PRE-FLIGHT, before any code: run `aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name solace-encounter-ledger` and `aws iam simulate-principal-policy` for PutItem as solace-lambda-exec. HANDOFF.md:495 says durable backing is 'unverified', both existing write sites are clinician-triggered and swallow LedgerUnavailable (triage.py:114-118, clinical_ai.py:495), and test_ledger_iam_policy.py:96-99 documents that the simulator once said implicitDeny on PutItem while the enforcement script printed success. If either check fails, every ledger write in the programme fails silently as a log line. This is one command and it should be the first thing done.

PRE-FLIGHT: measure one warm triage_ml.predict() on the deployed 2048 MB arm64 container and the serialized byte size of one ledger entry. Every number in the cost estimate and the per-tick census ceiling rests on these two, and neither exists anywhere in the repo — the only recorded duration is the 60 s timeout from the incident.

SHADOW DRY RUN: enable the rule for 24 hours against a synthetic hospital with 30 seeded encounters before enrolling a real one. Assert 288 heartbeat entries, zero errors, p99 duration under 20 s, and verify() ok on every chain. Then read the actual invoice line for that day before extending to 90.
designs.weakest_point:
The scheduler is correct, cheap and safe, and it will mostly have nothing new to score. That is the honest weakest point, and it is not a flaw in the scheduling design — it is a flaw in what the scheduling design sits on top of, which this design cannot fix and should not pretend to.

`triage_ml.predict()` is a deterministic function of (patient, vitals). `build_row` hard-codes every temporal feature — `arrival_hour=12`, `arrival_day="Monday"`, `arrival_season="winter"`, `shift="day"`, prior-visit counts 0 (`backend/services/triage_ml.py:326-334`) — so wall-clock time does not enter the feature vector at all. The patient half of the input (transcript, medical_info, language) is written once at intake and never mutated. The vitals half is a single `measured_vitals` JSON blob overwritten in place by the nurse-triggered refine-triage route (`backend/routers/triage.py:76`). There is no vitals time-series table in any of the five setup scripts, no FHIR Observation poller, no device stream, no HL7 ORU path that writes vitals. `services/ehr_copilot.py:79` reads `patient.get("vitals")`, a key nothing in the codebase ever writes.

So the input fingerprint changes exactly when a human types vitals into Solace. Between those moments, a 5-minute cadence re-scores byte-identical input and provably produces byte-identical output. My design handles this honestly — it records a `rescore_no_input_change` event rather than writing 288 identical predictions a day — but honesty about it does not make the cadence meaningful. The ≤5-minute number becomes a property of the scheduler, not of the clinical signal.

That has a direct consequence for the thing the programme exists to measure. Recognition delay is "Solace flagged this patient at T1, the team recognised it at T2". If Solace's input only refreshes when a nurse takes and enters vitals, then T1 is bounded below by the nurse's cadence, and the shadow system cannot recognise deterioration earlier than the humans whose data entry it depends on. The under-triage rate you compute at week 14 would largely re-measure the intake score, dressed up as continuous surveillance. Worse, it fails in the flattering direction: it will look like agreement.

It compounds with a second gap. Solace's own intake collects no vitals at all (`backend/services/triage.py:2-6` says so explicitly, and `_predict_trained` is called with three arguments at `:52`, so `vitals` defaults to None). My completeness gate will therefore refuse to score most encounters until a nurse runs refine-triage at least once. That refusal is the right behaviour — the alternative is a ledger full of "ESI 3, vitals normal" derived entirely from `triage_ml`'s silent imputation of `gcs_total=15`, `mental_status="alert"`, `shock_index=0.8` and the training-set medians — but it means the realistic day-one output of this scheduler is a large number of `score_refused_incomplete` events and a small number of real scores.

The fix is not in the scheduler. It is an ADT/vitals feed from the ED's EHR — and this design deliberately makes room for one: the roster's `last_vitals` and `inputs_snapshot` are the seam a feed would write into, and nothing else in the tick would change. I did not read `backend/routers/ehr.py`, `ehr_auth.py`, `services/hl7_v2.py` or `services/tefca_qhin.py`, so it is possible something there already carries ADT or observations; that is the first thing worth checking before enabling the rule, because it also supplies the real discharge signal my closure heuristic is substituting for.

Two smaller weaknesses I will not hide behind the first. (1) There is no departure marker anywhere in the schema — `backend/db/constants.py` has only `waiting` and `seen`, and 'seen' is first contact, not discharge — so 'for their whole length of stay' is implemented as a heuristic (patient row gone plus a stale window, or a 24 h cap) whose every decision is recorded as an `encounter_closed` event with a reason so week 14 can partition the cohort by it. The denominator of the under-triage rate depends on that heuristic being roughly right. (2) I am adding a table and a Lambda to a two-person team's estate, which is against my own instincts; I traded that for a hard concurrency ceiling and an IAM deny that make the two failure modes this project has actually suffered — an unbounded scheduled invocation, and a control that lived only in the AWS console — structurally impossible rather than merely documented.

designs.name: Tick–Claim–Commit: a dedicated shadow-scorer Lambda with a DynamoDB-arbitrated per-(encounter, tick) lease
designs.summary:
A separate Lambda function (`solace-shadow-scorer`), built from the same ECR image as `solace-api` but with `ImageConfig.Command = ["shadow_handler.handler"]`, driven by an **EventBridge Scheduler** schedule at `rate(5 minutes)` with a hard `EndDate`. It never touches `main.handler`, so PERF-002's `source == "aws.events"` warmup branch (backend/main.py:266) cannot swallow it and needs no constitutional amendment, and the deploy smoke test at scripts/deploy_container.py:174-184 keeps working unchanged.

Each invocation is a **tick**, identified by `<aws.scheduler.scheduled-time>` floored to the 300s bucket — the *intended* time, not wall clock, so a late or duplicated delivery carries the same `tick_id`. The tick enumerates the active census from a new sparse GSI on a new `solace-shadow-roster` table (a Query with an explicit KeyConditionExpression and a real `LastEvaluatedKey` loop — never a `.scan()`, never the unpaginated patients GSI at backend/db/storage.py:181-187).

Per encounter the loop is strictly **reconcile → claim → score → commit**:
1. **Reconcile** — if `last_claimed_tick > last_committed_tick`, the previous tick died between claiming and writing: append a `model="event"` ledger entry `{"event": "shadow_gap", "reason": "claimed_not_committed"}`. If `tick − last_committed_tick > 1`, append `{"event": "shadow_gap", "reason": "cadence_missed", "missed_from", "missed_to", "missed_ticks"}`. Every hole in the cadence becomes a row before any new score is written.
2. **Claim** — one conditional `UpdateItem` on the roster: `SET last_claimed_tick = :t` with `ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(last_claimed_tick) OR last_claimed_tick < :t"`. DynamoDB, not the process, arbitrates. A duplicate delivery, an overlapping slow tick, and a Lambda retry all lose the same CAS and do nothing.
3. **Score** — `storage.get_patient` (GetItem) + the enrolment snapshot on the roster row → completeness gate → `triage_ml.predict` → raise-only `triage_rules` floor → a validated `ShadowScore` → `encounter_ledger.record(model="shadow.triage_ml", ...)`. Insufficient input or `predict() is None` produce `model="event"` refusal/failure entries, never a silent skip and never a low-acuity score.
4. **Commit** — `SET last_committed_tick = :t`.

The whole tick body runs on a daemon thread joined with a 60s budget, exactly the `_run_warmup` shape at backend/main.py:253-257 (a between-steps deadline bounds the gaps, not the steps — the call that hung in 42abe22 was `_load()` and never returned to be checked), *plus* a per-encounter deadline check so the encounters not reached are recorded as gaps rather than lost. Budget 60s < function timeout 90s < cadence 300s, asserted by a test.

The shadow guarantee (requirement 6) is enforced three ways, not one: the scorer package never imports `db.storage`'s write functions or `services.workflows`; a derived-scope test with an **empty** allowlist proves the import closure cannot reach any egress leaf; and the scorer's IAM role carries an explicit `Deny` on `dynamodb:UpdateItem`/`PutItem` for `solace-patients` and `solace-notes`, so even a bug cannot write the ED board. `routers/encounters.py` timeline is additionally filtered to drop `model` values beginning `shadow.` — that clinician-authenticated endpoint is today a live path from a shadow score to a clinician screen and must be closed before the programme starts.

Three prerequisite fixes to shared code are part of this design, not optional follow-ups: **(a)** `encounter_ledger` allocates sequence numbers from a `ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1, ConsistentRead=True` tail read instead of loading the whole chain — this makes writes O(1) in chain length and kills the 1MB-page wedge that would otherwise permanently brick every boarding patient within days at 288 entries/day; **(b)** the SequenceTaken fallback `chain = _load_all(...) or chain + [entry]` (encounter_ledger.py:327) is removed — it fabricates a never-persisted entry that makes the ledger accuse itself of tampering after a cold start, which is fatal to the week-14 claim; **(c)** `_check_uncertainty` is tightened from key-presence to value validity so `{"coverage": None}` can no longer pass.
designs.trigger_mechanism:
**EventBridge Scheduler schedule** `solace-shadow-rescore` in schedule group `solace-shadow`:
- `ScheduleExpression="rate(5 minutes)"`, `ScheduleExpressionTimezone="UTC"`, `FlexibleTimeWindow={"Mode":"OFF"}` (the report measures minutes; jitter would corrupt recognition-delay arithmetic).
- `StartDate` = programme start, **`EndDate` = start + 91 days**. The 42abe22 warmer "ran unnoticed for weeks" because nothing could stop it but a human reading an invoice. This schedule expires on its own.
- `Target={"Arn": <scorer fn arn>, "RoleArn": "solace-shadow-scheduler-invoke", "Input": '{"shadow_tick": true, "hospital_ids": [...], "scheduled_time": "<aws.scheduler.scheduled-time>"}', "RetryPolicy": {"MaximumRetryAttempts": 0, "MaximumEventAgeInSeconds": 120}, "DeadLetterConfig": {"Arn": <sqs solace-shadow-dlq>}}`.

Scheduler over a classic EventBridge rule for one operational reason, not price (both are free at 288/day): `scripts/deploy_container.py:157-161` calls `events.put_targets(Rule="solace-warmer", Targets=[{"Id": "solace-lambda", ...}])` with no RetryPolicy and no DeadLetterConfig. `put_targets` replaces a target by Id, so the deploy script is itself a mechanism that silently erases target-level retry config. A Scheduler schedule lives in a different API surface (`boto3.client("scheduler")`, available in the pinned boto3==1.35.36) that no existing script can reach.

**Lambda function** `solace-shadow-scorer` — same ECR image digest as `solace-api`, `PackageType="Image"`, `ImageConfig={"Command": ["shadow_handler.handler"]}`, `Architectures=["arm64"]`, `Timeout=90`, `MemorySize=2048`, `Role="solace-shadow-exec"`, `Environment.Variables.SOLACE_MODE="aws"` (config.py:128-135 then refuses to boot if that is ever wrong, so the ledger can never silently write to an in-process dict). No API Gateway integration and no `apigateway.amazonaws.com` invoke permission is ever added.

Three cost controls set **in code**, in `scripts/deploy_shadow_scorer.py`, and asserted by an AST test so they cannot be quietly dropped the way the original ones were:
- `lam.put_function_event_invoke_config(FunctionName=..., MaximumRetryAttempts=0, MaximumEventAgeInSeconds=120, DestinationConfig={"OnFailure": {"Destination": <dlq arn>}})`
- `lam.put_function_concurrency(FunctionName=..., ReservedConcurrentExecutions=3)`
- the schedule's own RetryPolicy above (belt and braces — retries are zeroed at both the schedule and the function).

**SQS queue** `solace-shadow-dlq`, CMK-encrypted (alias/solace), 14-day retention, alarmed on depth > 0. A dropped tick becomes a queryable artifact instead of a void.

The separate function is the load-bearing choice. `backend/main.py:266` matches `event.get("source") == "aws.events"` — the exact field EventBridge stamps on every delivery — and returns `{"warm": true}` after a dry predict on a fake patient named "warm", never reaching Mangum. A schedule pointed at `solace-api` would show 100% success in CloudWatch while scoring nobody, and PERF-002 (CONSTITUTION.md:748-757, L1) pins that branch so it cannot be deleted. A separate function sidesteps the collision entirely and also buys an Errors metric that is not diluted by clinician API traffic, an independent timeout, and a reserved-concurrency blast cap that `solace-api` must not have.
designs.enumeration_strategy:
**No `.scan()` anywhere, and no reliance on `solace-patients` row existence.**

New table `solace-shadow-roster` (created in `scripts/setup_shadow.py`, using the same `_resolve_cmk_arn()` / `SSESpecification` pattern as scripts/setup_aws.py:56-62 for COMP-003, `BillingMode="PAY_PER_REQUEST"`, PITR on):
- Base key: `encounter_id` (S) HASH, no sort key. Point `GetItem` and point conditional `UpdateItem` — this is what the CAS claim writes to.
- Sparse GSI `active-index`: HASH `active_hospital` (S), RANGE `enrolled_at` (S), `ProjectionType="INCLUDE"`, `NonKeyAttributes=["last_claimed_tick","last_committed_tick","snapshot","enrolled_at"]`.
- `active_hospital` is written **only while the encounter is in the department** and `REMOVE`d on discharge. The GSI therefore contains the current census and nothing else — ~20-45 items at BSW McKinney scale, not the ~10,700 rows the roster accumulates over 90 days. Enumeration is O(census), not O(programme).
- `ttl` = `enrolled_at + 100 days` (90-day programme + the week-14 report window). The ledger stays TTL-free.

Enumeration per tick, in `backend/db/shadow_roster.py` (all boto3 lives here, per ARCH-002 — the scorer service calls this module, never boto3):

```
resp = table.query(IndexName="active-index",
                   KeyConditionExpression=Key("active_hospital").eq(hospital_id),
                   Limit=100)
while True:
    yield from resp["Items"]
    if "LastEvaluatedKey" not in resp: break
    resp = table.query(..., ExclusiveStartKey=resp["LastEvaluatedKey"])
```

An explicit `KeyConditionExpression`, an explicit `LastEvaluatedKey` loop, and a KEYS+INCLUDE projection rather than the ALL projection that makes the patients GSI drag transcripts and SHAP blobs. PERF-004's stated check ("hot paths use `.query()` with an explicit KeyConditionExpression") is satisfied on the merits, and its literal three-router scope is untouched.

The hospital list comes from `settings.shadow_hospital_ids` (config), never from a table. No cross-tenant enumeration primitive is added — `grep "def list_hospitals|def list_all"` returns nothing today and must keep returning nothing, or the SEC-008 hole that does not currently exist gets created.

**Why not the existing patients GSI.** `_ddb_query_patients_by_hospital` (backend/db/storage.py:181-187) is a single unpaginated `.query()` against an ALL-projection index; it silently truncates at 1MB and there is no `LastEvaluatedKey` anywhere in the backend. Patients it drops are indistinguishable from patients who left — which is precisely the population the under-triage rate is about. Worse, presence in that table is not evidence of presence in the department: TTL is 24h by default (storage.py:29) and **30 minutes once a clinician marks the patient seen** (routers/patients.py:190), and DynamoDB sweeps up to ~48h late. A boarding patient's row vanishes mid-stay on a nondeterministic schedule.

**Three consequences handled explicitly:**

1. *Durable encounter → hospital mapping.* The ledger item has no `hospital_id` (encounter_ledger.py:148-163) and the table has no GSI. Rather than adding a top-level attribute — which enters `_digest`'s hashed payload (encounter_ledger.py:234-249) and would invalidate `verify()` on every chain written before the change — the hospital is recorded inside the **enrolment event's `output` dict**: seq 1 is `model="event"`, `output={"event":"shadow_enrolled","hospital_id":...,"enrolled_at":...,"inputs_snapshot":{transcript, medical_info, language}}`. Hash payload shape unchanged, no verification break, no ledger GSI, no amendment to `scripts/iam_ledger_allow.json`, and `backend/tests/test_ledger_iam_policy.py:110-116` (`assert arn == LEDGER_ARN`) stays green. Enumeration for week 14 comes from the roster table, which is exactly the enumerable index of encounter_ids the ledger cannot provide.

2. *Scoring inputs outliving the patient row.* The roster row carries the immutable `snapshot` (transcript, medical_info, language — the four keys `triage_ml.build_row` reads off `patient`, per triage_ml.py:288-355), so a tick can score an encounter whose patient row has already been TTL'd. The same content is in the ledger's seq-1 enrolment event, so the roster's 100-day TTL does not lose evidence.

3. *TTL reconciliation, as a named compliance decision.* `backend/db/storage.py:_default_ttl` becomes shadow-aware (96h for hospitals in `settings.shadow_hospital_ids`, 24h otherwise) and `routers/patients.py:190` skips the 30-minute shortening for those hospitals. This directly widens the PHI retention footprint that patients.py:177-183 documents as a deliberate HIPAA-minimisation control, so it is a decision the deploying hospital's privacy office signs, not a config tweak. It is made **once, in the storage layer**, outside the scorer — the scorer itself never writes to the patient row at all.

**Departure signal.** There is none today: `db/constants.py` has only `waiting`/`seen`, and `seen` is first contact, not departure. `roster.discharge(encounter_id)` is the interface the census/ADT feed calls. Until one exists, the only departure signal is a backstop: any encounter with `now − enrolled_at > SHADOW_MAX_LOS_HOURS` (default 48) is auto-discharged by the tick, `active_hospital` is REMOVEd, and a `model="event"` entry `{"event":"shadow_discharged","reason":"auto_discharge_max_los"}` is written — so the roster cannot leak forever and the week-14 LOS figures are explicitly marked "backstopped, not observed" rather than silently wrong.
designs.idempotency:
**Five independent layers, because the ledger itself has no dedupe — `record()` allocates `seq = len(chain)+1` unconditionally, so a duplicate trigger appends a legitimately-numbered duplicate score and inflates the week-14 denominators.**

**1. Stable tick identity.** `tick_id` is derived from `event["scheduled_time"]`, populated by Scheduler's `<aws.scheduler.scheduled-time>` context attribute, floored to the 300s bucket and rendered ISO-8601 Z. It is the *intended* occurrence time, not wall clock. A delivery that arrives 40 seconds late, or twice, carries the same `tick_id`. If the field is absent (manual invoke, misconfiguration) the handler falls back to floored wall clock and stamps `tick_source:"wall_clock"` on every entry it writes, so the degradation is visible in the record rather than inferred.

**2. DynamoDB arbitrates the claim, not the process.** `roster.claim(encounter_id, tick)` is one conditional UpdateItem:
```
UpdateExpression="SET last_claimed_tick = :t, last_claimed_at = :now"
ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(last_claimed_tick) OR last_claimed_tick < :t"
```
`ConditionalCheckFailedException` means someone already owns this (encounter, tick) — skip, silently and correctly. This covers duplicate EventBridge deliveries (at-least-once, not exactly-once), two containers running concurrently, an overlapping slow tick, and a Lambda async retry, with one mechanism and no coordination. Reserved concurrency 3 permits overlap deliberately: a slow tick must not block the next one, and the CAS makes overlap harmless.

**3. Lambda retries are zero.** `MaximumRetryAttempts=0` at both the schedule and the function, so a "retry" is not an event that occurs. The CAS is the defence-in-depth if someone re-enables them.

**4. `tick_id` is inside the hash.** `output["tick_id"]` and `output["scored_at"]` are part of `_digest`'s payload (encounter_ledger.py:234-249 hashes `output`). Two things follow. First, an entry proves *when we looked*, not merely when the data was observed — necessary because `observed_at` stays pinned to the vitals observation time and `recorded_at` is deliberately outside the digest (encounter_ledger.py:234-249) and therefore not defensible evidence. Second, any duplicate that somehow slipped past the CAS is detectable and collapsible at report time by `(encounter_id, tick_id)` uniqueness. A test asserts that pair is unique across a simulated 200-tick run with injected duplicate deliveries.

**5. The score itself cannot disagree with itself.** `triage_ml.predict` is fully deterministic — `build_row` hard-codes every temporal feature (`arrival_hour=12`, `arrival_day="Monday"`, `arrival_season="winter"`, `shift="day"`, triage_ml.py:326-334), so wall clock does not enter the feature vector. Identical inputs give bit-identical outputs, and a dedupe never has to choose between two answers.

**Cold starts.** Nothing that matters lives in process memory. `last_claimed_tick` / `last_committed_tick` are DynamoDB attributes. Sequence allocation reads the real tail from DynamoDB with `ConsistentRead=True` before numbering (the read-through at encounter_ledger.py:206-217 exists precisely to stop a fresh container restarting at seq 1 and writing a second unlinked chain over the real one). A cold container loses nothing but time, and the time is bounded by the tick budget.

**Overlapping runs.** Safe by the CAS. Additionally, a container whose worker thread was abandoned by the budget join is **poisoned**: that thread may still hold `encounter_ledger._lock` (a single module-global lock held across the whole DynamoDB round trip, encounter_ledger.py:299-321), so the next invocation in the same container would block on it forever and be abandoned in turn — a poison spiral. The handler sets a module-level `_abandoned` flag when a join times out; on the next invocation, if the flag is set, it writes a `model="event"` gap entry for the current tick and then **raises**, so Lambda tears down the container and the stuck thread with it. With retries at 0 that costs exactly one Errors data point and no re-invocation, and the Errors alarm (threshold 0, not 5) surfaces it. The worker also carries a per-invocation `generation` token checked immediately before every ledger write, so a thread that thaws on a subsequent invocation exits instead of writing a stale entry. To stop the spiral at the source, `encounter_ledger` acquires its lock with `_lock.acquire(timeout=5)` and raises `LedgerUnavailable` on failure rather than blocking indefinitely.

**Partial data.** Never scored as normal. Missing vitals are silently replaced with clinically normal values inside `build_row` (`gcs_total or 15`, `mental_status or "alert"`, `shock_index if not None else 0.8`, weight/height/bmi `or 70/170/24`, triage_ml.py:346-351) and the `miss_*` indicator features are dead at inference because imputation runs before they are computed (triage_ml.py:366-370 vs train_triage_model.py:171-179). The model therefore cannot report its own input completeness and never will. The scorer measures it: `CORE_VITALS = {systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, heart_rate, respiratory_rate, temperature_c, spo2}`; a score is emitted only if ≥ `SHADOW_MIN_CORE_VITALS` (default 4 of 6) are present **and** `measured_vitals_at` is within `SHADOW_VITALS_MAX_AGE_MINUTES` (default 240). Otherwise a `model="event"` entry `{"event":"refused_insufficient_input","completeness":0.33,"missing":["spo2","respiratory_rate",...],"threshold":0.67}` — the refusal recorded as a refusal, never as a low-acuity score. `completeness` is stamped into `inputs` on every emitted score too, so the report can stratify by it.

failure_modes.mode: The tick never fires — schedule disabled, throttled by the concurrency cap, or the delivery lands in the DLQ.
failure_modes.handling: Nothing runs, so nothing self-heals in that moment; the gap is closed at the next successful tick. Per encounter, `tick − last_committed_tick > 1` produces one summarising ledger event `{"event":"shadow_gap","reason":"cadence_missed","missed_from","missed_to","missed_ticks"}` — one entry per contiguous gap, not one per missed tick, or a multi-hour outage across a full census would write tens of thousands of rows and become its own incident. For encounters discharged *during* the outage there is never a next tick, so `roster.discharge()` and the max-LOS auto-discharge both write `expected_ticks` vs `committed_ticks` into the discharge event: every encounter's shortfall is recorded at least once no matter when the outage falls. Out-of-band: DLQ depth alarm and an Invocations-below-expected alarm.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scorer.py::test_a_skipped_cadence_becomes_one_gap_event — run tick N, skip ticks N+1..N+11, run N+12; assert exactly one `shadow_gap` entry with missed_ticks == 11 and missed_from/missed_to bracketing the hole. test_a_discharge_during_an_outage_still_records_the_shortfall — discharge with no intervening tick; assert the discharge event carries expected_ticks > committed_ticks.

failure_modes.mode: The invocation dies between claiming a tick and writing the ledger entry (timeout, OOM, container reclaim, ledger throttle).
failure_modes.handling: This is the crash window the whole shape is built around, and it is why claim precedes score and commit follows the write. The roster is left with `last_claimed_tick > last_committed_tick`, which is a durable, unambiguous record that a tick was started and not finished. The next tick's reconcile step sees it and writes `{"event":"shadow_gap","reason":"claimed_not_committed","tick_id":<the lost tick>}` before doing anything else, then advances the commit pointer. A crash cannot produce a silent gap; it produces a labelled one.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scorer.py::test_a_crash_between_claim_and_commit_is_recorded — monkeypatch `encounter_ledger.record` to raise after the claim, run tick N, restore, run tick N+1; assert a `claimed_not_committed` event exists naming tick N.

failure_modes.mode: `encounter_ledger.record` raises `LedgerUnavailable` mid-batch (throttling, ResourceNotFoundException if the table was never created, IAM implicitDeny on PutItem).
failure_modes.handling: Not swallowed. routers/triage.py:114-118 swallows it correctly — the score is already in front of the clinician there — but in the shadow programme the ledger entry IS the product, so a swallowed failure means the week-14 report silently under-counts. The scorer catches per encounter, increments a process counter, attempts one gap event for that encounter, and continues to the next (one patient's throttled read must not stop the department). The counter is emitted as a CloudWatch EMF metric `ShadowLedgerWriteFailures` at the end of the tick — the audit.py `_write_failures` + /health pattern (lib/audit.py:41-50, main.py:100-110) adapted for a function with no HTTP surface, since a module-global counter in a separate Lambda is invisible to anything polling /health. Alarm at >0. If the gap event *also* fails, the tick raises at the end so the failure appears in Errors rather than as a clean 200.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scorer.py::test_one_patients_ledger_failure_does_not_stop_the_department — three encounters, middle one raises LedgerUnavailable; assert the first and third produced entries, the failure counter is 1, and the tick did not abort.

failure_modes.mode: A prediction is emitted with no calibrated uncertainty or no SHAP attribution — a bare number reaching the ledger.
failure_modes.handling: Structurally impossible at three layers. (a) `ShadowScore` is a frozen dataclass whose `__post_init__` rejects `esi_level` outside 1-5, an empty `conformal_set`, a `coverage` that is not a float in (0,1], an empty `coverage_source`, or an empty `top_features`; it is the only type `scorer._emit()` accepts and `_emit()` is the only place in the package that calls `record()`. (b) `encounter_ledger._check_uncertainty` is tightened from key-presence to value validity — today `{"coverage": None}` is accepted (encounter_ledger.py:261-265 only tests `"coverage" not in uncertainty`), which defeats the rule the entire ledger rests on. It now requires a numeric coverage in (0,1], a non-empty `uncertainty["conformal_set"]`, and a non-empty `output["top_features"]` for any model that is not exactly `"event"`. (c) an AST test asserts no `encounter_ledger.record(` call site exists in `backend/services/shadow/` outside `_emit`/`_emit_event`. NOTE: (b) is a deliberate breaking change — `test_encounter_ledger.py:46` passes `{"set": [2,3], "coverage": 0.9}` (wrong key name, no top_features) and `test_encounter_ledger_durability.py:52` passes `output={"esi_level": 3}`; those tests must be updated. routers/triage.py:96-112 already passes both `conformal_set` and `top_features`, so production callers are unaffected.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scorer.py::test_a_bare_number_cannot_reach_the_ledger — parametrized over coverage None/0/1.5/"0.9", empty conformal_set, empty top_features; assert ShadowScore raises ValueError and, separately, that record() raises MissingUncertainty for each. Plus test_no_record_call_outside_emit (AST).

failure_modes.mode: The model would down-triage an obvious life threat (traumatic amputation, not breathing, GSW) because it is trained on templated synthetic data and defaults over-confidently to ESI 3.
failure_modes.handling: `triage_rules.evaluate()` is applied to every re-score with the strict raise-only comparison copied from backend/services/triage.py:134 — `if shortcut is not None and shortcut.esi_level < esi_level` — never the unconditional form at routers/intake.py:192-194, which can *lower* acuity when an ESI-5 administrative rule matches. On a floor hit the entry records `source="safety_floor+<model source>"`, `conformal_set=[floored]`, `confidence=max(confidence, 0.97)` and the rule name in `output["clinical_flags"]`, matching services/triage.py exactly. This closes a real gap: routers/triage.py — the only path that writes to the ledger today — never imports triage_rules at all (line 20 imports only `encounter_ledger, triage_ml`), so every refined ESI in the ledger right now is unfloored. The floor runs on the enrolment snapshot's transcript, which does not change during the stay, so the floor's verdict is stable across ticks.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scorer.py::test_the_floor_can_only_raise_acuity — property test over the full cross product of model ESI 1-5 and every pattern in `triage_rules.RULES`; assert `floored <= model_esi` in all cases, including the ESI-5 administrative rules against a model output of ESI 1.

failure_modes.mode: The tick runs out of time before reaching every patient in the department (large census, cold start, slow DynamoDB).
failure_modes.handling: Two nested bounds. The whole tick body runs on a daemon thread joined with a `SHADOW_TICK_BUDGET_SECONDS=60` timeout — the `_run_warmup` shape at backend/main.py:253-257, chosen because 42abe22 records that a between-steps deadline check was written first and was useless: the call that hung was `_load()` and it never returned to be checked. Inside the loop, a monotonic deadline is checked before each encounter, and every encounter not reached gets `{"event":"shadow_gap","reason":"tick_budget_exhausted"}`. Encounters are visited in ascending `last_committed_tick` order, so the ones already starved are served first and no patient can be permanently starved by census growth. Budget 60s < timeout 90s < cadence 300s.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scheduler_is_bounded.py::test_a_hung_predict_returns_inside_the_budget (monkeypatch predict to sleep 300s; assert the handler returns in < 65s and reports it gave up); ::test_unreached_patients_are_recorded (budget 0.1s, 10 encounters; assert every unreached encounter has a tick_budget_exhausted event); ::test_the_budget_is_well_under_the_function_timeout (assert SHADOW_TICK_BUDGET_SECONDS <= 60 and < SHADOW_FUNCTION_TIMEOUT).

failure_modes.mode: A worker thread abandoned by the budget join holds the ledger's global lock; the next invocation in the same warm container blocks on it forever and is abandoned in turn.
failure_modes.handling: A poison spiral that would silently stop the entire programme while CloudWatch showed clean 200s. Three defences: `encounter_ledger` acquires its module lock with `_lock.acquire(timeout=5)` and raises `LedgerUnavailable` instead of blocking; the handler sets a module-level `_abandoned` flag on a join timeout and, on the next invocation, writes a gap event and then **raises** so Lambda destroys the container and the stuck thread with it (retries are 0, so this costs one Errors data point and no re-invocation); and the worker checks a per-invocation `generation` token immediately before every ledger write, so a thread that thaws on a later invocation exits rather than writing an entry attributed to the wrong tick.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scheduler_is_bounded.py::test_a_poisoned_container_kills_itself — force an abandonment, invoke again, assert a gap event was written and the handler raised; ::test_a_thawed_worker_does_not_write — call the worker body with a stale generation and assert record() was never reached.

failure_modes.mode: A long-stay encounter's ledger chain outgrows DynamoDB's 1MB Query page, wedging the encounter permanently.
failure_modes.handling: The single failure mode that most directly destroys the week-14 report, and at 288 entries/day it is a day-two problem, not a week-two one. Today `_load_all` (encounter_ledger.py:182-187) issues one Query with no `LastEvaluatedKey` loop; once the chain crosses a page the read truncates, `seq = len(chain)+1` comes back too low, the conditional PutItem fails, all 8 attempts burn, and `record()` raises `LedgerUnavailable` forever on every container — while `verify()` reports `ok=True` on the truncated prefix, so the record silently stops growing while claiming to be intact. Fixed at the root rather than worked around: `_chain()` is replaced for the write path by `_tail()`, a `query(ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1, ConsistentRead=True)`. `seq = tail.seq + 1` and `prev_hash = tail.entry_hash` are both obtainable from the tail alone, so writes become O(1) in chain length. `timeline()`, `latest()` and `verify()` still need the full chain and get a proper `LastEvaluatedKey` loop; `verify()` additionally takes the tail seq and reports `reason="truncated read"` when the walked length falls short, so a partial read can no longer masquerade as an intact chain.
failure_modes.test: test_encounter_ledger_durability.py::test_a_thousand_entry_chain_still_appends (fake table, 1000 entries, assert append 1001 succeeds and issues exactly one Limit=1 tail query); ::test_verify_detects_a_truncated_read (truncate _load_all to 3 of 5; assert ok is False with reason 'truncated read' — this currently returns ok=True).

failure_modes.mode: A SequenceTaken retry fabricates an entry that was never persisted, so the ledger accuses itself of tampering after a cold start.
failure_modes.handling: encounter_ledger.py:327 reads `chain = _load_all(encounter_id) or chain + [entry]`. When the re-read returns empty, the `or` branch inserts the entry that just *failed* to persist. The warm container then reports 2 entries with `verify().ok == True` while only 1 row reached the table, and after a container recycle the same encounter reports `ok=False, broken_at=1, reason='sequence gap'` on a record nobody touched — the worst possible outcome for a tamper-evidence claim, and it is now on a path that runs 288 times a day per patient instead of once per clinician click. The fallback is removed: on SequenceTaken the writer re-reads the tail, and if the tail read returns nothing while a conditional check just failed, it raises `LedgerUnavailable` rather than inventing state. The in-memory cache is also switched to tail-only in aws mode and capped at 2048 entries via an `OrderedDict` LRU, since `_entries` (encounter_ledger.py:90) has no eviction outside the test-only `reset()` and would otherwise grow monotonically inside a 2GB function whose model working set already peaks at 642MB.
failure_modes.test: test_encounter_ledger_durability.py::test_a_failed_persist_is_never_cached — _persist raises SequenceTaken once, _load_all returns []; assert LedgerUnavailable is raised and the in-memory state matches the store exactly; ::test_the_cache_is_bounded — write 3000 encounters, assert len(_entries) <= 2048.

failure_modes.mode: A shadow score becomes visible to a clinician or reaches the EHR.
failure_modes.handling: Enforced at three layers because a code-review promise is not a control. (1) The scorer never writes the patient row — `refined_esi_level` is projected by routers/patients.py:46-48 and :101-108 and PatientCard.tsx:20-21 displays it *in preference to* `esi_level`, so writing it is writing the ED board; and it never calls `workflows.engine.fire()`, one call to which reaches send_sms, send_slack_webhook, http_webhook, create_clinician_note, set_patient_field, ehr_write and notify (services/workflows/actions.py:375-520). The scorer is therefore not built by copying refine_triage's body, which does both. (2) `test_shadow_has_no_egress.py` computes the forward import closure from `services.shadow.scorer` using the SEC-004 fixed-point algorithm (test_consent_gate.py:118-164) and asserts the intersection with a derived egress-leaf set is empty, with an `ALLOWED_EGRESS` dict whose correct steady state is `{}`; plus a qualified-callee allowlist (`storage.get_patient`, `storage.list_patients_for_hospital`, `triage_ml.predict`, `triage_ml.model_version`, `triage_rules.evaluate`, `encounter_ledger.record`, `audit.record`, `shadow_roster.*`, `tenancy.belongs_to`) — read-only on the patient store, append-only on the ledger. (3) The `solace-shadow-exec` role carries an explicit `Deny` on `dynamodb:UpdateItem`/`PutItem`/`BatchWriteItem` for `solace-patients` and `solace-notes`. An IAM Deny beats every Allow, so even a bug cannot write the ED board. Separately, `GET /api/{hospital}/encounters/{pid}/timeline` (routers/encounters.py:56-80) is clinician-authenticated and returns every ledger entry including its `output.esi_level` — that is a live path from a shadow score to a clinician screen today and is filtered to drop entries whose `model` starts with `shadow.`. `verify()` still walks the full chain: integrity is not clinical content.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_has_no_egress.py — the closure assertion with an empty allowlist, a staleness test killing dead exemptions, a floor assertion so a broken matcher cannot pass vacuously, and a driven test that seeds one patient, spies on storage.update_patient / storage.put_patient / storage.add_note / sms.send / email.send_email / httpx.Client.post / workflows.engine.fire / lib.claude.messages_create, runs exactly one tick, asserts every spy has zero calls and that timeline gained exactly one entry that verifies. Plus test_the_clinician_timeline_hides_shadow_entries.

failure_modes.mode: Vitals are absent or stale, so the model scores a deteriorating patient as if their vitals were normal.
failure_modes.handling: A refusal event, never a score. See the completeness gate in `idempotency`. Also fixed here: `observed_at`. routers/triage.py:93 passes `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` while its own comment at :85-87 says it must be the time the vitals were taken — and the report's central claim is measured in minutes from observation. `routers/triage.py` starts writing `measured_vitals_at` alongside `measured_vitals` (line 76), and both it and the scorer pass that as `observed_at`. For an encounter with no vitals at all, `observed_at = enrolled_at` and the entry is a refusal, not a score, so no ESI is ever attributed to a timestamp it did not come from.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scorer.py::test_stale_vitals_are_refused_not_scored (vitals 5 hours old; assert a refused_insufficient_input event and no shadow.triage_ml entry); ::test_observed_at_is_the_vitals_timestamp (assert the recorded observed_at equals measured_vitals_at, not the tick time).

failure_modes.mode: `triage_ml.predict()` returns None — artifacts missing from the deployed image, or any internal exception.
failure_modes.handling: Never treated as 'nothing to write'. predict() catches every exception and returns None (triage_ml.py:646-648), the identical value it returns when artifacts are absent (:592), so a scheduler that skips on None produces a silent ledger gap indistinguishable from a healthy patient. The scorer writes `{"event":"score_failed","reason":"predict_returned_none","model_version_source":<from model_version()>}`. `triage_ml.model_version()` returns `("no-artifacts", "absent")` when nothing loads (triage_ml.py:552-586), which the handler checks once at tick start — if the version source is `absent`, the whole tick emits `score_failed` events and raises, so a container deployed without artifacts.pkl is loud rather than producing 288 quiet no-ops a day. buildspec.yml treats the artifacts S3 copy as best-effort (`|| echo WARN artifacts.pkl missing`), so this is a realistic deployment state.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_scorer.py::test_a_none_prediction_is_recorded_as_a_failure; ::test_a_container_with_no_artifacts_fails_loudly (model_version returns ('no-artifacts','absent'); assert the tick raises and every active encounter got a score_failed event).

failure_modes.mode: A deploy silently removes the retry / concurrency / DLQ protections, re-arming the 42abe22 amplification.
failure_modes.handling: The lasting lesson of 42abe22 is not matplotlib — it is that two of its four fixes live only in the AWS console, so nothing in the repo can prove today that retries are still 0 or the warmer is still disabled. Every control here is set in `scripts/deploy_shadow_scorer.py` and asserted by an AST test that parses that script and fails if `MaximumRetryAttempts=0`, `MaximumEventAgeInSeconds`, `ReservedConcurrentExecutions`, `DeadLetterConfig` or the schedule `EndDate` disappear. `scripts/verify_shadow_infra.py` reads the live `get_function_event_invoke_config`, `get_function_concurrency` and `get_schedule` and exits non-zero on drift, and is run as the last step of every deploy. `scripts/deploy_container.py` is amended in the same change to call `put_function_event_invoke_config` on `solace-api` too — that function's delete-and-recreate branch at :85-90 destroys function-level EventInvokeConfig, so the original mitigation is one Zip-mode deploy away from evaporating, and to pass a `RetryPolicy` in `point_warmer`'s `put_targets` (:157-161), which currently erases any console-set policy on every deploy.
failure_modes.test: test_shadow_infra_is_codified.py — AST-parse scripts/deploy_shadow_scorer.py and assert each keyword is present with the expected literal; assert the scorer function is never passed to `apigw.create_integration` or `lam.add_permission(Principal='apigateway.amazonaws.com')`; assert scripts/deploy_container.py calls put_function_event_invoke_config.

designs.cost_estimate:
**Sizing.** BSW McKinney, 43,301 ED visits/year ≈ 119/day (HANDOFF.md:783); at ~4h LOS the average census is ~20 and the peak ~45.

**Lambda invocations: 8,640/month (288/day), flat.** One tick per 5 minutes that loops the department in-process — *not* per-patient fan-out, which at this census would be ~172,800 invocations/month, each risking the cold start that in 42abe22 measured 642MB and 60+ seconds, for identical output.

**Duration.** Per encounter, warm: GetItem ~8ms + claim UpdateItem ~10ms + `predict()` ~50ms (unmeasured — see unknowns) + tail Query ~8ms + conditional PutItem ~12ms + commit UpdateItem ~10ms ≈ 100ms. A 20-encounter tick ≈ 2s; a 45-encounter peak tick ≈ 4.5s. Cold starts add the `artifacts.pkl` unpickle (unmeasured; bounded by the same 60s budget, and a blown budget is a recorded gap, not a runaway).

**Monthly bill at 120 patients/day:**
- Lambda compute: 8,640 × 5s avg × 2048MB = 86,400 GB-s × $0.0000133334 (arm64) ≈ **$1.15**
- Lambda requests: 8,640 × $0.20/M ≈ **$0.00**
- Ledger writes: 20 × 288 = 5,760/day at ~3KB (SHAP `top_features` + probabilities + inputs) = 3 WCU each → 518k WCU/month × $1.25/M ≈ **$0.65**
- Roster ops (claim + commit + GSI page): ~17,500/day, ~1 unit each ≈ **$0.30**
- Patient GetItems: 5,760/day, eventually-consistent 4KB read ≈ **$0.05**
- Ledger + roster storage: ~1.5 GB/month growing to ~4.5 GB by day 90 × $0.25/GB ≈ **$0.40**
- SQS DLQ + CloudWatch alarms/EMF: ≈ **$0.75**
- **Total ≈ $3.30/month, ≈ $10-12 for the whole 90-day programme.**

**Why this cannot repeat the warm-ping bill — arithmetically, not by intention.**

The 42abe22 mechanism was: no time budget → every invocation ran to the 60s timeout → a timeout is a failure → Lambda's default two async retries → 360 pings/day became 1,080 minute-long 2GB invocations, ~18 hours of billed compute a day, $14.56 of a $28.76 monthly bill, on a function whose API Gateway bill that month was one cent. Nothing capped it, and nothing detected it: `solace-lambda-errors` (setup_cloudwatch_alarms.py:48-54) fires above 5 errors per 5 minutes and the incident ran at ~3.75, so it sat under the threshold for weeks until someone read an invoice.

Six controls, each of which alone would have prevented it:

1. **`MaximumRetryAttempts=0`** at both the schedule's `RetryPolicy` and the function's `EventInvokeConfig` — the 3× multiplier is gone. Set in code, AST-asserted, and re-verified against live config on every deploy, unlike the original which exists nowhere in this repo.
2. **`ReservedConcurrentExecutions=3`** — a physical ceiling. Absolute worst case, with every invocation running to the full 90s timeout and never completing: 288/day × 90s × 2GB × 30 days = 1.56M GB-s ≈ **$20.70/month, hard-capped**. Overspend becomes arithmetically impossible rather than merely unlikely. The old design had no ceiling at all. This also converts the already-deployed `solace-lambda-throttles` alarm (Sum(Throttles) > 0) into a working runaway detector.
3. **A 60s in-handler budget on a joined daemon thread**, under a 90s function timeout, under a 300s cadence. A hang costs 60s once, not 90s three times, and it is *recorded* as a gap rather than reported as success.
4. **Schedule `EndDate` = start + 91 days.** The programme physically cannot outlive its own window. The warmer ran for weeks because only a human could stop it.
5. **Alarms that would actually have caught it**, since the current set demonstrably would not: Errors ≥ 1 in 15 min on the scorer function specifically (threshold 0, not 5 — 3.75 errors per 5 minutes is exactly what slipped through), Duration p99 > 60s, Invocations outside 250-350/day (a cadence that speeds up is the runaway signature), DLQ depth > 0, and an AWS Budgets / EstimatedCharges alarm, of which this repo has none. The DynamoDB alarms are fixed in the same change: setup_cloudwatch_alarms.py:73-80 alarms on `UserErrors` dimensioned by `TableName`, but `UserErrors` is an account-and-region aggregate with no such dimension, so with `TreatMissingData="notBreaching"` all ten sit permanently in OK on no data. They move to `ThrottledRequests` / `ReadThrottleEvents` / `WriteThrottleEvents` and gain `solace-encounter-ledger` and `solace-shadow-roster`, neither of which is in the list today.
6. **A separate function**, so the scorer's Errors and Duration metrics are not diluted by clinician API traffic and its concurrency cap does not throttle patient-facing requests.

**test_shadow_scorer.py — idempotency, four scenarios in one file.** (a) Deliver the same tick_id twice; assert exactly one ledger entry and that the second delivery lost the CAS. (b) Run two `tick()` calls concurrently against the same fake roster; assert exactly one entry per encounter. (c) Deliver ticks out of order (N+1 then N); assert the stale tick is rejected by the `last_claimed_tick < :t` condition. (d) Assert `(encounter_id, tick_id)` is unique across a simulated 200-tick run with injected duplicate deliveries — the report-time dedupe key must actually be a key.

**test_shadow_scorer.py — the gap-event family.** (a) crash between claim and commit → `claimed_not_committed` naming the lost tick; (b) skip ticks N+1..N+11 → exactly one `cadence_missed` with `missed_ticks == 11`; (c) budget exhausted mid-loop → `tick_budget_exhausted` for every unreached encounter, and assert starved encounters are visited first on the next tick; (d) discharge during an outage → the discharge event carries `expected_ticks > committed_ticks`. The invariant under test across all four: **for every (encounter, tick) in the programme window, the ledger contains either a score, a refusal, a failure, or a gap event — never nothing.** Write that as a single sweep assertion over a simulated 3-day, 30-patient run with randomly injected crashes, throttles and budget exhaustion.

**test_shadow_scheduler_is_bounded.py — the 42abe22 shape, restated for the tick.** Monkeypatch `triage_ml.predict` to sleep 300s; assert the handler returns in under 65s and reports it gave up rather than dressing failure as success (mirrors test_warmup_is_bounded.py:63,79). Assert `SHADOW_TICK_BUDGET_SECONDS <= 60` and strictly less than the function timeout, which is strictly less than the cadence. Assert a poisoned container writes a gap event and then raises so Lambda destroys it, and that a thawed worker with a stale generation token never reaches `record()`.

**test_encounter_ledger_durability.py — the pagination wedge and the fabrication bug, which are the two defects that most directly destroy the week-14 report.** (a) A 1000-entry chain still appends, and does so with exactly one `Limit=1` tail query rather than a full-chain read. (b) `verify()` on a truncated `_load_all` returns `ok=False, reason='truncated read'` — it currently returns `ok=True, checked=3` on a partial read of 5, which is an incomplete record claiming to be intact. (c) `_persist` raises SequenceTaken once while `_load_all` returns []; assert LedgerUnavailable and that the in-memory state matches the store exactly. Today this fabricates an entry, reports `verify().ok is True` with 2 entries while 1 row exists, and after a cold start reports `ok=False, broken_at=1, reason='sequence gap'` — the ledger accusing itself of tampering on a record nobody touched. (d) `_entries` stays under the LRU cap after 3000 encounters.

**A real end-to-end run against real DynamoDB, because the durable path has zero coverage today.** All 37 existing ledger tests pass in 0.13s with no AWS credentials and `solace_mode` at its 'local' default; `_persist` returns at line 144 before touching boto3, so nothing has ever exercised the write path. Add an opt-in integration test (`SOLACE_IT=1`) against a scratch table that: (i) proves `attribute_not_exists(encounter_id) AND attribute_not_exists(seq)` is actually accepted by DynamoDB on this composite key — no test and no recorded live run exercises it, and test_encounter_ledger_durability.py:22 documents a *different* expression than the code uses, so the two have drifted; (ii) runs two concurrent writers on one encounter and asserts the chain verifies; (iii) simulates a cold start by clearing `_entries` mid-run and asserts numbering continues rather than restarting at 1.

**test_shadow_infra_is_codified.py.** AST-parse scripts/deploy_shadow_scorer.py and assert `MaximumRetryAttempts=0`, `MaximumEventAgeInSeconds`, `ReservedConcurrentExecutions`, `DeadLetterConfig` and the schedule `EndDate` are each present as literals; assert the scorer is never passed to `apigw.create_integration` or `lam.add_permission(Principal='apigateway.amazonaws.com')`; assert scripts/deploy_container.py calls `put_function_event_invoke_config`. This exists because the original 42abe22 mitigations lived only in the console and nothing in the repo can prove today that they still hold.

**Pre-flight checks against the live account, before any of the above is trusted.** Four things the repo cannot answer and that would each invalidate the programme silently: `aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name solace-encounter-ledger` (if it was never created, every production write has been failing with ResourceNotFoundException, wrapped as LedgerUnavailable at encounter_ledger.py:331 and swallowed by both callers, visible only as a log line); `aws iam simulate-principal-policy` for `dynamodb:PutItem` on the ledger as solace-lambda-exec (test_ledger_iam_policy.py:96-99 records that this exact failure already happened once — the simulator said implicitDeny while the script printed success); `aws events describe-rule --name solace-warmer` to confirm it is still DISABLED; and `aws lambda get-function-event-invoke-config --function-name solace-api` to confirm retries are still 0. Then measure two numbers that size everything: real `triage_ml.predict()` wall time on a warm 2048MB arm64 container, and the serialized byte size of one ledger entry.
designs.weakest_point:
**The scheduler will be provably correct and clinically empty, because the census, vitals and discharge feeds it depends on do not exist anywhere in this repo — and every safety mechanism I designed makes that emptiness *more* faithfully recorded rather than less likely.**

Three specifics, in descending order of how badly they hurt:

1. **There is no vitals time series.** The only persisted vitals are `measured_vitals`, a single JSON blob overwritten in place by the nurse-triggered refine-triage route (routers/triage.py:76). Intake collects none at all (services/triage.py:2-6 says so in its docstring). There is no FHIR Observation poller, no device stream, no HL7 ORU path writing vitals to a patient row; `services/ehr_copilot.py:79` reads `patient.get("vitals")`, a key nothing ever writes. So a 5-minute cadence has, in the general case, **no new input to score**. My completeness gate handles this honestly — it emits `refused_insufficient_input` rather than scoring an imputed-normal patient as ESI 3 — but the consequence is that at week 14 the ledger could be a near-perfect, hash-chained, tamper-evident record of 780,000 refusals. That is a better outcome than 780,000 fabricated normals, and it is not a product.

2. **There is no departure signal, so "for their whole length of stay" is a guess.** `db/constants.py` has exactly two statuses, `waiting` and `seen`, and `seen` is first contact — in an ED that fires early while the patient boards for hours. There is no `discharged_at`, no disposition *event* (the `disposition` attribute is a json.dumps of the AI's *recommendation*), and no arrival timestamp distinct from record-write time. My max-LOS backstop stops the roster leaking and labels every auto-discharge as backstopped, but that means the denominator of the recognition-delay calculation — how long each patient was actually present and scoreable — is a 48-hour ceiling, not an observation. Under-triage rate is a ratio, and I have made its numerator trustworthy while leaving its denominator approximate.

3. **Every patient row in this system came through Solace's own intake form.** `routers/intake.py:302` is the only caller of `storage.put_patient` in the entire application. "Re-score EVERY patient currently in the department" describes a population the system cannot currently see at all, none of whom would have a `consent_granted_at` for `consent.for_patient()` to read (lib/consent.py:89-98) if the hospital's counsel decides a consent basis is required — a question the code cannot answer and that I have deliberately left as a config decision rather than picking for them.

**Two smaller weaknesses I am not going to dress up.**

The SHAP attribution on every ledger entry explains **fold 0's LightGBM booster only** — `_shap_top_features` does `b = boosters[0]` (triage_ml.py:651-663) while the ESI itself may come from `_stacked_predict`. Requirement 2 is met literally: a SHAP attribution is present and structurally required. It is not an explanation of the model that produced the number, and an auditor who reads the code will notice.

And the conformal coverage figure is a placeholder on today's artifacts. `scripts/train_triage_model.py:550-551` writes `conformal_q_hat` and `conformal_q_hat_noisy` but never `conformal_coverage`, so `triage_ml.py:618-620` falls through to `DEFAULT_CONFORMAL_COVERAGE = 0.90` with `coverage_source="declared_default"`. I have made that source tag mandatory in every entry, so the ledger says "nobody wrote the calibration target down" rather than quietly asserting 90%. But "every score carries a conformal uncertainty set" is, until a retrain writes a real calibration target, a claim about a set whose stated coverage has never been measured.

**Finally, one thing I chose that a reasonable reviewer would push back on.** I write a ledger entry every tick — 288 per patient per day — even when the inputs are byte-identical to the previous tick, because my prior is that a gap nobody noticed is worse than an outage and I want "we looked at 14:35 and the answer was still ESI 3" to be a row rather than an inference. That costs ~780k items over the programme, forced me to fix the ledger's sequence allocator to make it survivable, and produces a record that is mostly repetition. Suppressing unchanged scores would be cheaper and would read better — but it would make an absent entry ambiguous between "unchanged" and "we failed and did not notice", which is the exact ambiguity this whole design exists to eliminate.

designs.name: SHADOW-CADENCE — sharded roster with a conductor/worker split
designs.summary:
A dedicated two-function scheduler, fully separate from `solace-api`, driven by a durable shard-partitioned roster table that is the system's only definition of "currently in the department".

**Shape.** EventBridge Scheduler (`rate(1 minute)`, StartDate/EndDate pinned to the 90-day window) invokes a tiny **conductor** Lambda. The conductor does one `Query` against a programme table to get enrolled hospitals, then enqueues one SQS message per `(hospital_id, shard)` on a deterministic stagger so each shard is visited every 4 minutes. A **worker** Lambda (same ECR image, different `ImageConfig.Command`) consumes one message at a time, queries a sparse `due-index` for that one shard, and scores what is due. Nominal cadence 4 min, hard SLO 5 min, 60s of jitter headroom.

**Why not one tick-Lambda that loops the department.** That design dies the moment the pilot succeeds. At 50 hospitals × 25 census = 1,250 predicts per tick; at ~300ms warm that is 375s against a 60s timeout. Sharding is the difference between a pilot artefact and a product. Cost stays linear in (hospitals × census) because enumeration is an index seek over *due* encounters, never over all patients.

**Why the roster, not `solace-patients`.** `solace-patients` cannot answer "who is here": TTL is 24h by default (`backend/db/storage.py:29`), collapses to 30 minutes once a clinician marks the patient seen (`backend/routers/patients.py:190`), and DynamoDB sweeps up to ~48h late (`backend/routers/patients.py:197-199`). Row existence is not evidence of presence and row absence is not evidence of departure. `db/constants.py` has exactly two statuses, `waiting` and `seen`, and neither is a departure marker. So the roster carries its own enrolment/departure lifecycle and its own immutable input snapshot, and the patient row becomes a *refresh* source rather than the source of truth.

**Compute path.** `triage_ml.predict()` → raise-only safety floor → completeness gate → `encounter_ledger.record()`. Nothing else. No `storage.update_patient`, no `workflows.engine.fire()`, no route, and no module that reaches `services.transcription`, `services.tts`, `lib.claude` or `services.voice_agent.tts_cache` — which keeps the whole path outside SEC-004's derived scope (`CONSTITUTION.md:90`) and at pure local CPU cost.

**Ledger fixes shipped as part of this.** Persistence moves to `backend/db/ledger_store.py`, fixing the ARCH-002 L1 violation at `backend/services/encounter_ledger.py:125-129` rather than adding a twelfth one. Sequence allocation switches from "read the whole chain" to a tail read (`Query ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1, ConsistentRead=True`), which kills the 1MB-truncation wedge at `encounter_ledger.py:182-187`, removes the need for the unbounded `_entries` cache (`:90`), and deletes the fabrication bug at `:327` where a failed write is inserted into the in-process chain. `hospital_id` joins the item and the digest — conditionally, so pre-existing chains still verify.
designs.trigger_mechanism:
**Two new Lambda functions on the existing ECR image, neither of which is `solace-api`.**

`backend/main.py:266` claims every event carrying `source == "aws.events"` for the warmup branch and returns `{"warm": true}` without reaching Mangum. PERF-002 (`CONSTITUTION.md:748-757`) pins that behaviour as an L1 rule, so it cannot be edited away, and the deploy smoke test at `scripts/deploy_container.py:174-184` depends on it. A scheduled rule pointed at `solace-api` would dry-predict on a fake patient named "warm" (`backend/main.py:236-241`), return 200, and score nobody while CloudWatch showed 100% success. The complementary failure is just as bad: a constant-`Input` target with neither `warmup` nor `source` falls through to Mangum, which raises `RuntimeError` (`mangum/adapter.py:69-75`) because no inferer matches — an async invocation failure, i.e. exactly the retry-amplified error class from 42abe22.

So: separate functions, separate entrypoint file, no collision.

1. **`solace-shadow-conductor`** — `ImageConfig.Command = ["shadow_handler.conduct"]`, 128MB, timeout 30s, `ReservedConcurrentExecutions=1`.
2. **`solace-shadow-worker`** — `ImageConfig.Command = ["shadow_handler.work"]`, 2048MB (matches the 642MB model working set recorded in 42abe22 with CPU headroom), timeout 120s, `ReservedConcurrentExecutions=6`.

`Dockerfile.lambda` keeps `CMD ["main.handler"]`; the two new functions override it via `ImageConfig`. One image, one build, three functions.

**Schedule.** EventBridge Scheduler (not a classic rule) named `solace-shadow-conductor`:
- `ScheduleExpression="rate(1 minute)"`, `FlexibleTimeWindow={"Mode":"OFF"}`
- `StartDate` / `EndDate` = the 90-day programme window. The 42abe22 warmer ran for weeks because nothing but an invoice could stop it; this one expires on its own.
- `Target.RetryPolicy = {"MaximumRetryAttempts": 0, "MaximumEventAgeInSeconds": 60}`
- `Target.DeadLetterConfig.Arn` = `solace-shadow-dlq`
- `Target.Input = {"solace_shadow": "conduct", "programme_id": "shadow-v1"}` — the discriminator key is `solace_shadow`, never `warmup`, never bare `source`.

Scheduler is chosen over a classic rule because retry policy, DLQ, and the start/end window are first-class properties of the schedule itself rather than split across target config and function config — and because `scripts/deploy_container.py:157-161` demonstrates the hazard of the split: `put_targets` with the same `Id` and no `RetryPolicy` silently erases whatever was set in the console.

**Fan-out.** Conductor → SQS `solace-shadow-ticks` (standard queue), redrive `maxReceiveCount=2` → `solace-shadow-dlq`, `VisibilityTimeout=720` (6× the worker timeout). Lambda event-source mapping with `BatchSize=1`, `MaximumConcurrency=6`, `FunctionResponseTypes=["ReportBatchItemFailures"]`.

SQS rather than `lam.invoke(InvocationType='Event')` specifically because async invoke is the retry-amplification surface that cost $14.56. SQS gives a bounded receive count, a real DLQ, queue depth as a first-class backpressure signal, and decouples the trigger cadence from worker concurrency. At 43,200 messages/month it is inside the free tier.

**Async invoke config, set in code on both functions:**
```python
lam.put_function_event_invoke_config(
    FunctionName=fn, MaximumRetryAttempts=0, MaximumEventAgeInSeconds=60,
    DestinationConfig={"OnFailure": {"Destination": dlq_arn}},
)
```
This is the single most important line in the design. The identical setting from 42abe22 exists nowhere in this repo (`grep` for `MaximumRetryAttempts|put_function_event_invoke_config|MaximumEventAge` returns zero hits), and `scripts/deploy_container.py:89` deletes the function on the Zip→Image path, which discards `EventInvokeConfig` entirely. It lives in `scripts/setup_shadow_scheduler.py`, is re-asserted on every run, and is asserted by a test.

**Kill switches, three of them, in decreasing latency:** the `enabled` flag on the programme row (stops a hospital within 60s, no deploy); the Scheduler `EndDate`; and a hard `if now > PROGRAMME_END: return` in `shadow_handler.conduct` so a schedule someone re-enables by hand still cannot run past the window.

`shadow_handler.py`'s first executable statement is `log_redaction.install()` — `backend/main.py:34` is the only thing that installs it today, and a separate entrypoint that never imports `main` would ship raw `pt-<hex>` ids to CloudWatch. `backend/lib/log_redaction.py:19-25` only catches hyphenated UUID4, `Bearer <tok>` and `intake_token=<tok>`, so the worker additionally follows the `backend/lib/audit.py:83-90` pattern: log the action and the count, never the item.
designs.enumeration_strategy:
No `.scan()` anywhere, and no reliance on `solace-patients` for the census.

**New table `solace-shadow-roster`** (created with the solace CMK per COMP-003, PAY_PER_REQUEST, PITR on, matching `scripts/setup_aws.py:56-63`):
- PK `shard` (S) = `f"{hospital_id}#{zlib.crc32(encounter_id.encode()) % SHARDS:02d}"`
- SK `item_kind` (S) — `"cadence"` for the hot, frequently-updated row; `"snapshot#<encounter_id>"` for the cold PHI blob. Splitting them matters for cost: DynamoDB bills `UpdateItem` WCU on the *post-update item size*, so keeping the 4-minutely-updated cadence row under 1KB instead of 6KB is a 6× write saving that compounds over 90 days.
- Sparse GSI `due-index`: HASH `shard`, RANGE `next_due_at` (ISO8601 Z — lexicographic order is chronological order), `ProjectionType=KEYS_ONLY`. Deliberately not `ALL`: `scripts/setup_aws.py:90` projects ALL on `hospital_id-created_at-index` and that is precisely why the dashboard drags `transcript`/`shap_values`/`ai_processing_log` to build an 18-field summary and hits the 1MB page early.

**The due query** — the hot path, run once per shard visit:
```python
resp = table.query(
    IndexName="due-index",
    KeyConditionExpression=Key("shard").eq(shard) & Key("next_due_at").lte(now_iso),
    Limit=BATCH_LIMIT,          # 40
    ExclusiveStartKey=start,    # real pagination loop
)
```
Explicit `KeyConditionExpression`, explicit `Limit`, and a genuine `while "LastEvaluatedKey" in resp` loop — the thing that exists nowhere in the current backend (`grep -rn 'LastEvaluatedKey\|ExclusiveStartKey' backend/` returns zero matches, which is why `backend/db/storage.py:181-187` silently truncates the department at 1MB). Then one `GetItem` per due encounter for the cadence row and, on cold read, the snapshot row.

**The index is sparse, and that is the scaling property.** `next_due_at` is *removed* (not set to a sentinel) when an encounter departs, is quarantined past its backoff, or the programme ends. Departed encounters therefore cost exactly zero in the due query forever. The query never scans population, only work.

**Hospital enumeration — new table `solace-shadow-programme`:**
- PK `programme_id` (S) = `"shadow-v1"`, SK `hospital_id` (S)
- attrs: `shards`, `cadence_seconds`, `starts_at`, `ends_at`, `enabled`, `max_los_hours`, `completeness_threshold`

One paginated `Query` on `programme_id="shadow-v1"` returns every enrolled hospital. 50 rows is ~5KB. No scan, no cross-tenant iteration primitive added anywhere — `grep -rn "def list_hospitals|def list_all" backend/db/ backend/services/` returns zero hits today and this design keeps it that way.

**Per-tenant isolation is structural, not procedural.** The partition key literally embeds `hospital_id`, so a worker handed `shard="A#02"` physically cannot read hospital B's rows — the `KeyConditionExpression` forbids it. Belt and braces: the worker asserts `tenancy.belongs_to(row, hospital_id)` (`backend/lib/tenancy.py:62-71`) on every roster row and on every patient row before scoring, and on mismatch records a `model="event"` entry with `kind="tenant_mismatch"` rather than scoring. It does not call `tenancy.require_patient`, which logs a raw `patient_id` at WARNING (`backend/lib/tenancy.py:53-56`) that survives redaction for `pt-<hex>` ids.

**Enrolment and departure.** `services/shadow/roster.enrol(...)` is called from `backend/routers/intake.py` (one service call after `storage.put_patient` at :302) when the hospital's programme row is `enabled`. It snapshots the immutable scoring inputs — `transcript`, `medical_info`, `language` — into the snapshot row. Departure comes from, in priority order: an explicit departure call (none exists yet, see weakest point), `departed_at` from an ADT feed if one is ever wired, or `enrolled_at + max_los_hours` (default 36h) as a backstop that writes `kind="departed_max_los"` to the ledger so the record says *why* scoring stopped rather than going silent.

`status == "seen"` explicitly does **not** depart an encounter. First contact is not departure, and the 30-minute TTL at `backend/routers/patients.py:190` treating it as one is the single most dangerous existing assumption for this programme.

**Retention.** Roster `ttl` is refreshed to `now + 30 days` on every claim, so an active encounter can never be swept mid-stay the way `solace-patients` rows are. On departure the worker does one `UpdateItem` that `REMOVE`s the snapshot and vitals and `SET`s `ttl = departed_at + 180 days`, leaving identifiers and counters only. This is what makes the week-14 report computable: the roster is the durable `encounter_id → hospital_id` index that `solace-encounter-ledger` lacks (no `hospital_id` in the item at `encounter_ledger.py:148-163`, no GSI at `setup_aws.py:170-180`, no `Scan` in `scripts/iam_ledger_allow.json`). Adding a GSI to the ledger would require amending that policy to cover `/index/*`, which breaks the deliberate guard at `backend/tests/test_ledger_iam_policy.py:110-116` — so the roster carries the index instead and that test stays intact.

Additionally `hospital_id` is added to the ledger item itself, so the ledger is self-describing even if the roster expires. It is included in `_digest()` **only when present**, so every pre-existing chain hashes exactly as before and still verifies. A fixture test pins that.

PERF-004's literal scope is three router files (`CONSTITUTION.md:771-780`), so a scheduler is outside its letter — but the rule's stated check is `.query()` with an explicit `KeyConditionExpression` in hot paths, and this design satisfies the check, not just the scope. The only `.scan(` on DynamoDB in the repo remains `scripts/rotate_pins.py:51`, an offline script.
designs.idempotency:
Four independent layers, because each one fails differently.

**1. The claim is a compare-and-swap on the roster (primary).** Before any scoring, the worker claims the encounter:
```python
table.update_item(
    Key={"shard": shard, "item_kind": "cadence"},
    UpdateExpression=("SET next_due_at = :next, lease_until = :lease, "
                      "last_tick_id = :tick, #ttl = :ttl ADD tick_count :one"),
    ConditionExpression=("next_due_at = :expected AND encounter_id = :eid AND "
                         "(attribute_not_exists(lease_until) OR lease_until < :now)"),
)
```
`ConditionalCheckFailedException` means another worker already holds this tick. That is a normal outcome, not an error: the loser logs a counter and moves on. This makes duplicate SQS delivery (at-least-once, always), two overlapping conductor ticks, and a straggler worker whose message reappeared after visibility timeout all converge on exactly one score per encounter per tick. Claim happens *before* the predict, so two workers never both reach the ledger.

**2. Tick identity in the ledger, checked against the tail (secondary).** `tick_id = int(now_epoch // cadence_seconds)`. The worker already reads the ledger tail to allocate `seq`, so the dedupe check is free: if `tail.model == "triage_ml.shadow"` and `tail.output["shadow"]["tick_id"] == tick_id`, skip the append. This catches the case the CAS cannot — a worker that claimed, wrote to the ledger, then died before the roster update landed, and whose message was redelivered.

**3. The score itself is deterministic (structural).** `triage_ml.predict()` hard-codes every temporal feature — `arrival_hour=12`, `arrival_day="Monday"`, `arrival_season="winter"`, `shift="day"` (`backend/services/triage_ml.py:326-334`) — so `is_night`, `is_weekend`, `hour_sin`, `hour_cos` are constants at serve time and wall-clock never enters the feature vector. Identical inputs give a bit-identical ESI. A leaked duplicate can inflate a count; it cannot change a clinical claim.

**4. Week-14 dedupe on `(encounter_id, tick_id)` (final).** The analysis deduplicates before computing denominators. Layers 1-3 should make this a no-op; if it is ever not a no-op, that fact is itself evidence and should be reported.

**Cold starts.** The ledger's read-through at `encounter_ledger.py:206-217` exists precisely so a fresh container does not restart numbering at 1 and write a second unlinked chain. This design keeps that guarantee and strengthens it: `seq` is derived from a strongly-consistent tail read (`ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1, ConsistentRead=True`) on **every** append in AWS mode, never from the in-process `_entries` dict. The in-memory chain becomes local-mode-only. That removes the unbounded-growth problem at `encounter_ledger.py:90` and removes the fabrication bug at `:327` — where `chain = _load_all(...) or chain + [entry]` inserts a never-persisted entry into the in-process chain, producing a container that reports `verify() == ok, checked=2` while only one row reached the store, and the same encounter reporting `ok=False, broken_at=1, reason='sequence gap'` after recycle. A ledger that accuses itself of tampering on a record nobody touched is the worst possible outcome for a tamper-evidence claim, and it must not survive into a 90-day programme.

**Lambda retries.** Structurally absent rather than merely configured away. `MaximumRetryAttempts=0` on both functions; SQS `maxReceiveCount=2` → DLQ; and the worker **never returns a failure for a per-patient problem** — every per-patient failure is recorded in the ledger and in the roster counters and the invocation returns success. The only thing that fails an invocation is an infrastructure fault (credentials, table missing), which is exactly what belongs on the DLQ. This is the property that makes the 3× multiplier from 42abe22 impossible rather than unlikely.

**Overlapping runs.** The conductor holds `ReservedConcurrentExecutions=1`, so two conductor ticks cannot run concurrently. The worker's concurrency is capped at 6 by reserved concurrency *and* by `MaximumConcurrency=6` on the event-source mapping. Two workers landing on the same shard is possible (redelivery) and safe — the CAS resolves it.

**Partial data.** Handled as a first-class outcome, not an exception: see `refused_low_completeness` in the failure modes. A re-score with no fresh vitals must not be recorded as a confident normal reading.

Also re-asserts (1) on `solace-api` in `scripts/deploy_container.py`, since that setting currently exists only in the live account and `scripts/deploy_container.py:89` deletes the function on one path.
failure_modes.test: `test_shadow_scheduler_is_bounded.py::test_retries_are_pinned_to_zero_in_code` — AST-parses `scripts/setup_shadow_scheduler.py`, finds every `put_function_event_invoke_config` and `create_schedule` call, and asserts `MaximumRetryAttempts == 0` and a `MaximumEventAgeInSeconds` is present on each; `test_reserved_concurrency_is_set_on_both_functions`; `test_the_schedule_carries_an_end_date`.
