failure_modes.mode: An invocation hangs and runs to the function timeout (`_load()` blocking on a cold container, a wedged DynamoDB call, a pathological predict)
failure_modes.handling: Copies `backend/main.py:253-258` exactly: each predict runs on a daemon thread joined with a `PER_PATIENT_BUDGET` (2.5s) timeout, and the whole tick body runs under `INVOCATION_BUDGET = min(context.get_remaining_time_in_millis()/1000 - 10, 90)`. Not a deadline checked between steps — 42abe22 records that the between-steps version was written first and was useless, because the call that hung was `_load()` itself and it never returned to be checked. The runaway thread is not killed (Python cannot) but Lambda freezes the container on handler return, so billing follows the handler. A budget-exceeded predict increments `consecutive_failures` and writes a `cadence_missed` event with `reason="predict_timeout"`.
failure_modes.test: `test_shadow_scheduler_is_bounded.py::test_a_hung_predict_does_not_consume_the_invocation` — monkeypatches `triage_ml.predict` to `time.sleep(60)`, runs one tick, asserts wall-clock elapsed < 5s, asserts the handler returned, and asserts a `cadence_missed` ledger event with `reason="predict_timeout"` was written.

failure_modes.mode: Ledger chain exceeds a 1MB Query page — the encounter is permanently wedged, every write burns all 8 seq attempts and raises `LedgerUnavailable` forever, while `verify()` reports `ok=True` on the truncated prefix
failure_modes.handling: `backend/services/encounter_ledger.py:182-187` is an unpaginated `Query`, and at 15 scores/hour with SHAP attributions in every entry a boarding stay reaches the boundary in days, not months. Two fixes: `db/ledger_store.read_tail()` uses `ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1, ConsistentRead=True` so append is O(1) and can never truncate; `db/ledger_store.read_all()` has a real `LastEvaluatedKey` loop for `timeline()`/`verify()`. `verify()` additionally gains an expected-length check so a truncated read reports `ok=False, reason="truncated read"` instead of claiming an incomplete record is intact.
failure_modes.test: `backend/tests/services/test_ledger_long_chains.py` — writes 400 entries against a fake table that enforces a 1MB page limit, then asserts entry 401 appends cleanly, `timeline()` returns 401 entries, and `verify().ok is True`. Second case: a deliberately truncated `read_all` must produce `ok=False`, not `ok=True, checked=3`.

failure_modes.mode: Two workers score the same encounter in the same tick — duplicate SQS delivery, overlapping ticks, or a message reappearing after visibility timeout
failure_modes.handling: Conditional `UpdateItem` claim on the roster CAS'ing `next_due_at` plus a lease, executed *before* the predict. The loser gets `ConditionalCheckFailedException`, treats it as a normal outcome, and skips. Secondary defence: the tail read that allocates `seq` also checks `tail.output.shadow.tick_id`, so a worker that died between the ledger write and the roster update cannot double-append. This also avoids the ledger's own contention path entirely — `_MAX_SEQ_ATTEMPTS = 8` retries at `encounter_ledger.py:115` should never be consumed, because there is only ever one writer per encounter per tick.
failure_modes.test: `backend/tests/services/test_shadow_scorer.py::test_two_workers_on_one_tick_produce_one_entry` — runs two `score_encounter` calls concurrently against a shared fake roster+ledger, asserts exactly one ledger append and that the second returns `skipped_already_claimed`.

failure_modes.mode: Poison-pill patient — one encounter fails every single run forever, burning a slot in every tick for the rest of the 90 days
failure_modes.handling: `consecutive_failures` on the roster row, reset to 0 on any success. At 3: write `model="event"` `{"kind":"scoring_quarantined","failures":3,"error_class":"..."}`, set `next_due_at = now + 1h` (exponential backoff to a 4h cap). At 10: write `{"kind":"scoring_abandoned"}`, `REMOVE next_due_at` so the encounter leaves the sparse index, and depart it. It never fails silently and it never consumes an unbounded number of cycles. The `error_class` is a type name only — never an error string, which could carry a transcript fragment.
failure_modes.test: `test_shadow_scorer.py::test_a_patient_that_always_fails_is_quarantined_then_abandoned` — a patient whose `predict` always returns `None`, driven through 12 ticks; asserts quarantine at 3 with a backoff, abandonment at 10, `next_due_at` absent afterward, and that both transitions are ledger events.

failure_modes.mode: ML inference slower than the cadence — backlog builds and the department is scored at 12-minute intervals while the ledger claims 4
failure_modes.handling: SQS queue depth is the backpressure signal (there is no such signal in a fire-and-forget design). The worker processes until its deadline and then returns; unprocessed encounters keep their un-CAS'd `next_due_at` and are picked up next visit, where the claim path detects `now > previous_due + 90s` and writes a `cadence_missed` event *before* the score. The worker never re-enqueues itself — no recursion, no self-amplification. Operationally: a `solace-shadow-queue-depth` alarm at `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > shards × 2` for 2 periods, and `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage > 240s`. Scaling response is more shards, not more concurrency per shard.
failure_modes.test: `test_shadow_scorer.py::test_a_late_tick_records_a_miss_before_the_score` — advances the clock past `next_due_at + grace`, runs one tick, asserts ledger entries in order `[event:cadence_missed, triage_ml.shadow]` and that `missed_ticks` incremented on the roster.

failure_modes.handling: The roster snapshot is authoritative for the immutable inputs (`transcript`, `medical_info`, `language`), captured at enrolment, with `ttl` refreshed to `now + 30 days` on every claim. `storage.get_patient()` is a *refresh* source for vitals only; when the row is gone the scorer proceeds from the snapshot and stamps `output.shadow.input_source = "roster_snapshot"` and `vitals_age_seconds` on the entry, so the week-14 analysis can see exactly which scores ran on stale inputs. This avoids raising the patient-row TTL, which `backend/routers/patients.py:177-183` documents as a deliberate HIPAA-minimisation control — the retention decision moves to a new store with its own justified lifetime rather than weakening an existing control.
failure_modes.test: `test_shadow_scorer.py::test_scoring_survives_a_deleted_patient_row` — enrols, deletes the patient row, runs a tick; asserts a ledger entry was still written and that it carries `input_source == "roster_snapshot"` and a non-null `vitals_age_seconds`.

failure_modes.mode: A department of patients with no fresh vitals scored as if their vitals were normal — the model silently substitutes clinically normal values and cannot report that it did
failure_modes.handling: This is the quietest and most damaging mode. `build_row` replaces every absent vital with a normal value — `gcs_total or 15`, `mental_status or "alert"`, `shock_index` → 0.8, weight/height/bmi → 70/170/24 (`backend/services/triage_ml.py:346-351`) — and the `miss_*` indicator features are dead at inference because imputation runs before they are computed (`triage_ml.py:366-370` vs `scripts/train_triage_model.py:171-179`), so they are always 0. The returned dict carries no completeness field at all. So the scorer computes completeness itself, outside `predict()`: the fraction of the 16 `vitals` keys that are genuinely present and fresher than `MAX_VITALS_AGE` (default 4h). Below `completeness_threshold` (default 0.4, per-hospital) it **refuses to emit a score** and instead records `model="event"` `{"kind":"refused_low_completeness","completeness":0.31,"present":[...],"vitals_age_seconds":...}`. This satisfies the acceptance bar at `docs/strategy/2026-07-30-product-strategy.md:302` ("refuse to emit when input completeness is below a stated threshold"), for which no threshold exists in the code today.

failure_modes.handling: The current gate is key-presence only: `_check_uncertainty` (`encounter_ledger.py:253-265`) accepts `{"coverage": None}` — verified by execution. Two changes. designs.cost_estimate:
**Sizing.** 120 patients/day, mean LOS ~5h → mean census 25, peak ~50. Cadence 4 min nominal → ~75 scores per encounter → ~9,000 scores/day. `SHARDS = 4` per hospital.

**Lambda invocations/month**
| Function | Rate | /month |
|---|---|---|
| conductor | `rate(1 minute)` | 43,200 |
| worker | 4 shards × 15 visits/hr × 24h = 1,440/day | 43,200 |
| **total** | | **~86,400** |

**Monthly cost (arm64, us-east-1)**
- Conductor: 43,200 × 0.3s × 0.125GB = 1,620 GB-s → **$0.02** + $0.009 requests
- Worker compute: 43,200 × 3s × 2GB = 259,200 GB-s → **$3.46** + $0.009 requests
- Worker cold starts: ~40/day × 15s × 2GB = 36,000 GB-s → **$0.48**
- DynamoDB ledger writes: 9,000/day × ~4KB (4 WCU) = 1.08M WRU/month → **$1.35**
- DynamoDB ledger tail reads: 9,000/day strongly-consistent `Limit=1` = 270k RRU → **$0.07**
- DynamoDB roster: 9,000 claims/day on a sub-1KB cadence row + 1,440 index queries/day → **$0.40**
- SQS: 43,200 messages/month → **$0** (free tier is 1M)
- Ledger storage growth: 9,000 × 4KB = 36MB/day → 3.2GB over 90 days → **$0.80/month** by the end
- CloudWatch Logs at 14-day retention: **~$0.30**

**≈ $7/month at one hospital.** For calibration: the 42abe22 warmer cost **$14.56/month** to warm nothing.

**At 50 hospitals** (same per-hospital census): 200 shards → 2.16M worker invocations/month, ~$170 Lambda + ~$100 DynamoDB ≈ **$270/month**. Linear in (hospitals × census), because the due query is an index seek over *work*, not over population, and the sparse index means departed encounters cost zero forever. There is no term that grows with the number of patients ever enrolled.

---

**Why this cannot repeat 42abe22 — the five specific mechanisms, not a promise**

The incident chain was: matplotlib rebuilt its font cache on a read-only FS on every cold start → the warm path had no time budget so it ran to the full 60s timeout → a timeout is a failure → Lambda's default **two async retries** tripled it → 360 pings/day became 1,080 minute-long 2GB invocations, none of which ever completed. Two of the four fixes landed in the repo; the other two live only in the AWS console, which is why nothing today can prove retries are still 0.

1. **The multiplier is set to zero in committed code, and a test asserts it.** `put_function_event_invoke_config(MaximumRetryAttempts=0, MaximumEventAgeInSeconds=60)` on both functions, `RetryPolicy` on the Scheduler target, `maxReceiveCount=2` on the SQS redrive — all in `scripts/setup_shadow_scheduler.py`, all AST-asserted by `test_shadow_scheduler_is_bounded.py`. The repo currently returns **zero hits** for `MaximumRetryAttempts|put_function_event_invoke_config|MaximumEventAge`, and `scripts/deploy_container.py:89` deletes the function on the Zip→Image path, discarding `EventInvokeConfig`. The same script now re-asserts it for `solace-api` too.

2. **The multiplier's *input* is also removed.** A timeout only amplifies if the invocation fails. The worker returns success for every per-patient failure — failures become ledger events and roster counters, not invocation errors. Only an infrastructure fault fails an invocation, and that goes to a DLQ with an alarm on it. In 42abe22 *every single invocation* errored (1,080/1,080); here a per-patient error rate of 100% still produces a 0% invocation error rate.

3. **Spend has a physically enforced ceiling.** `ReservedConcurrentExecutions`: conductor 1, worker 6. Worst case if both were pinned at 100% for a full month: conductor 1 × 0.125GB × 2.592M s = 324k GB-s = **$4.32**; worker 6 × 2GB × 2.592M s = 31.1M GB-s = **$415**. That is a bounded, statable number rather than an unbounded one, and it converts the already-deployed `solace-lambda-throttles` alarm (`scripts/setup_cloudwatch_alarms.py:55-61`, `Sum(Throttles) > 0`) into a working runaway detector — which it is not today, because nothing in the repo sets reserved concurrency anywhere.

4. **No invocation can run to its timeout.** Per-predict budget 2.5s and per-invocation budget `min(remaining - 10s, 90s)`, both enforced by a daemon thread joined with a timeout — the pattern at `backend/main.py:253-258`, chosen because the commit records that the between-steps deadline check was written first and was useless against a `_load()` that never returned.

5. **The alarms that missed it are fixed, and a budget exists.** New alarms on the scheduler functions specifically: `Errors >= 1` per 5 min (vs the `> 5` at `setup_cloudwatch_alarms.py:48-54` that the incident's ~3.75/5min slipped under), `Duration p99 > 0.6 × timeout`, `Invocations > 1.5 ×` the 86,400/month envelope, `DLQ ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0`, `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage > 240s`. Plus an **AWS Budgets alarm at $25/month with Cost Anomaly Detection** — the repo has no billing alarm of any kind today, and manual invoice review is how 42abe22 was found. Separately, the ten DynamoDB alarms at `setup_cloudwatch_alarms.py:73-80` are fixed: they alarm on `UserErrors` dimensioned by `TableName`, but `UserErrors` is an account-level aggregate with no `TableName` dimension, so with `TreatMissingData=\"notBreaching\"` all ten sit permanently OK on no data. They move to `ThrottledRequests`/`WriteThrottleEvents`, and `solace-encounter-ledger` — the table the entire programme writes to — is added, having been absent from the list entirely.

6. **It expires.** Scheduler `EndDate`, a handler hard-kill past `PROGRAMME_END`, and a per-hospital `enabled` flag. The warmer ran for weeks because nothing could stop it but a human noticing a bill.

**Explicitly not used: provisioned concurrency.** `scripts/enable_provisioned.py:144` sets PC=1 at 2048MB on a `live` alias — an always-on charge (~$45/month) unrelated to invocation count, and `scripts/deploy_container.py:23` (`ALIAS = None`) contradicts it about whether it is even active. A shard visited every 4 minutes stays warm on its own; paying to guarantee that is the wrong trade for a background job with no latency SLO.

designs.weakest_point:
**This design builds an industrial-grade delivery mechanism for a signal that does not change.**

There is no vitals time series in this system. `measured_vitals` is a single JSON blob overwritten in place on the patient row (`backend/routers/triage.py:76`), written only when a clinician manually submits the refine-triage form. There is no FHIR Observation poller, no device stream, no HL7 ORU path that writes vitals. And `triage_ml.predict()` is deterministic — `build_row` hard-codes `arrival_hour=12`, `arrival_day="Monday"`, `arrival_season="winter"`, `shift="day"` (`backend/services/triage_ml.py:326-334`), so wall-clock time never enters the feature vector.

Put together: **re-scoring the same patient every 4 minutes produces a bit-identical ESI, 75 times per encounter, until a human happens to type new vitals into a form.** The ledger will accumulate ~9,000 entries/day of which perhaps a few dozen carry a new value. "Recognition delay" measured against a constant is not a measurement. The week-14 under-triage rate would mostly be a statement about the single intake-time score, dressed up in 675,000 ledger rows.

And I chose to build the cadence anyway. That is the honest weakness — not an oversight, a trade I made. A cheaper design (score on input-change events, plus a 30-minute heartbeat) would produce the same clinical evidence at roughly a tenth of the write volume and a tenth of the complexity: no shards, no leases, no SQS, no miss detector. What it could not do is *prove the cadence held*, and "we looked at every patient every four minutes and here is the tamper-evident chain that shows it" is the auditable claim the programme is actually selling. I picked provable cadence over efficiency. If the vitals feed never lands, that was the wrong call and the sharding machinery was waste.

**Its twin, which makes it worse.** "Every patient currently in the department" is a population this system cannot see. `backend/routers/intake.py:302` is the only caller of `storage.put_patient` in the entire application — a patient row exists only if that patient completed Solace's own intake form. I checked for an alternative: `backend/routers/ehr.py` has search, lookup-by-patient, write-back and patient-match but no ADT ingest, and `backend/services/hl7_v2.py` has no A01/A03/A04 handling. So the roster's enrolment source is a self-selected subset, its `arrival_at` is record-write time rather than ED arrival (`backend/db/storage.py:104`), and its departure is a 36-hour timeout rather than a discharge event. The under-triage rate computed at week 14 would be about Solace's intake population, not the department's — and no amount of scheduler correctness fixes a denominator that is measuring the wrong set.

**What I would do about it.** Both problems are one dependency: an ADT + Observation feed from the ED's EHR. That feed is the gating deliverable for the shadow programme, and it should be built and validated *before* this scheduler ships, not alongside it. The design is deliberately structured so that lands cleanly — enrolment, departure and vitals refresh are three service calls on `services/shadow/roster.py` with no other coupling, so wiring an ADT consumer to them is additive. But I want to be plain: **the scheduler is the easy half.** If it ships first, the most likely outcome is 90 days of a beautifully instrumented, cryptographically chained, cadence-proven record of the same number written down 675,000 times.

**Two smaller weaknesses I will not hide.** (1) The design touches `encounter_ledger.py` substantially — tail-based sequencing, a moved persistence layer, a changed digest — and that module has **zero test coverage of its durable path** today (all 37 tests pass in 0.13s with no AWS credentials and `solace_mode` at its "local" default). I am refactoring the load-bearing component of a tamper-evidence claim against tests that have never exercised the code being refactored. The long-chain and digest-compat tests above are written to close that, but they are new tests validating a new implementation — there is no golden record from production to check against, and I could not determine whether any production ledger rows exist at all. (2) `conformal_coverage` is a placeholder. `scripts/train_triage_model.py:550-551` writes `conformal_q_hat` but never `conformal_coverage`, so every entry ships `coverage=0.90` with `coverage_source="declared_default"` (`triage_ml.py:481, 618-620`). Requirement 2 says a bare number must be structurally unable to reach the ledger, and this design enforces that — but a calibrated-looking 0.90 that nobody calibrated is a bare number wearing a coat. The `coverage_source` tag is the only thing standing between the week-14 report and a false precision claim, and the fix is a retrain that records its own calibration target, not anything in this scheduler.

verdicts.design_name: Shadow Tick — one dedicated Lambda, one disabled-by-default EventBridge rule, one roster table
fatal_flaws: ENROLMENT SILENTLY DROPS PATIENTS — the cursor is unsound against the real schema. backend/db/storage.py:25 is `_now_iso()` with `timespec="seconds"`, so `created_at` has ONE-SECOND resolution, and the design queries `created_at > :since` with a strict `>` and advances the cursor to max(created_at) seen. Interleaving A (same-second collision): patients P1 and P2 both get created_at="2026-08-11T14:23:07Z"; the tick's Query at 14:23:07.4 returns only P1 (P2's put_patient lands at 14:23:07.8); cursor advances to ...07Z; the next tick queries `> ...07Z` and P2, sitting at exactly ...07Z, is excluded FOREVER. Interleaving B, worse and not rare: GSI reads are ALWAYS eventually consistent and DynamoDB gives no ordering guarantee on index propagation. P1 (created_at ...07Z) propagates to hospital_id-created_at-index at 14:23:10.5; P2 (created_at ...09Z) propagates at 14:23:09.1. The tick queries at 14:23:10.0, sees only P2, advances the cursor to ...09Z, and P1 is permanently invisible to every future tick. The design asserts verbatim that the cursor is 'advanced to max(created_at) actually seen, never to now, so nothing is skipped' — that claim is false. The dropped patient gets no roster item, no ledger entry, no cadence_gap and no encounter_closed; they are indistinguishable from a patient who never existed, which is precisely the population the under-triage rate is about. Fix is cheap and absent: subtract a lookback (cursor minus 2 ticks) and lean on the `attribute_not_exists(sk)` conditional put that is already there.

SHADOW SCORES ARE WRITTEN INTO THE CLINICAL ENCOUNTER'S OWN HASH CHAIN, and every downstream problem below flows from that one choice. encounter_id == patient_id everywhere (routers/triage.py:91, routers/clinical_ai.py:483, routers/encounters.py:74), and the design's own driven test asserts `encounter_ledger.timeline(pid)` gained one entry — same chain. Consequences, all concrete: (a) GET /api/{h}/encounters/{pid}/timeline (routers/encounters.py:56) returns every entry to any authenticated clinician at that hospital; the design's mitigation is to filter `model.startswith("shadow_")` out of the response. (b) `_serialize` (routers/encounters.py:35-52) emits `seq`, `prev_hash` and `entry_hash` per entry, and the endpoint's own docstring says these exist so 'somebody who does not trust us can recompute the chain themselves'. Filtering leaves seq 1,26,51... with prev_hash values that do not link, so an external verifier recomputing the displayed chain gets 'sequence gap'/'broken link' for every enrolled patient. The programme destroys the tamper-evidence property of the clinical record for exactly the cohort it studies. (c) GET .../verify (routers/encounters.py:83) returns `checked` = raw chain length; an enrolled patient shows ~25+/day against ~1 for everyone else, so enrolment and cadence are inferable with no entry content at all. Filtering entries does not fix a count. Using a separate encounter_id namespace (`shadow#<patient_id>`) would have made this whole class disappear — require_patient() would 404 the chain, verify() would stay honest, and the idempotency bug below would not exist.

THE `model="event"` ENTRIES DEFEAT THE LEAK FILTER AND ONE OF THEM IS A CLINICAL NUDGE. The uncertainty exemption at encounter_ledger.py:253-255 is an exact string match on `"event"`, so cadence_gap, score_refused_incomplete, rescore_no_input_change, encounter_closed and score_failed MUST be spelled `model="event"` — and therefore none of them match `model.startswith("shadow_")`. All five pass straight through the design's own filter into the clinician timeline. `{"kind": "score_refused_incomplete", "present": [...], "missing": ["spo2", "respiratory_rate"]}` rendered on a clinician's screen is a prompt to go take vitals on that patient. That is the shadow programme influencing care, which is the one thing the 90 days must not do. The design never notices that its exemption requirement and its filter requirement are in direct contradiction.

THE IDEMPOTENCY KEY IS UNREADABLE THE MOMENT ANY NON-SHADOW WRITER TOUCHES THE CHAIN, and the design's own tail-only optimization is what makes it unreadable. Duplicate suppression is `tail = tail(E); if tail.output.get("tick_id", -1) >= tick_id: skip`, where tail() is Query(ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1). Two live writers append to that same chain with no tick_id in `output`: routers/triage.py:90-113 (clinician refine-triage) and routers/clinical_ai.py:482-500 (ai-override event). Interleaving: at 14:20:03 tick N writes seq=41 (tick_id=N); at 14:20:07 a nurse submits refine-triage, writing seq=42 with no tick_id; at 14:20:11 a duplicate EventBridge delivery (at-least-once is documented, not theoretical) re-runs tick N; tail is seq=42, `.get("tick_id", -1)` returns -1, `-1 >= N` is False, so the patient is scored and recorded AGAIN at seq=43 with tick_id=N. Two prediction entries for one tick, both cryptographically valid, denominator inflated. The same defect corrupts gap detection in the opposite direction: `tail_tick_id < tick_id - 1` evaluates `-1 < N-1`, which is true, so every tick that follows any clinician entry writes a bogus cadence_gap claiming `missed_ticks` ≈ tick_id (a number in the tens of thousands by day 90) onto the chain the recognition-delay report is computed from. The correct read is 'last SHADOW-authored entry', which `latest(encounter_id, model=...)` at encounter_ledger.py:349-357 already provides — but it walks the whole chain via `_chain()`, i.e. exactly the O(n) read the tail-only rewrite exists to eliminate. The design's own fix and its own idempotency scheme are mutually exclusive and it does not see the collision.

`record()` IS NOT INTERNALLY IDEMPOTENT, SO A LOST RESPONSE PRODUCES A DUPLICATE SCORE THE tick_id CHECK CANNOT SEE. The conditional put is `attribute_not_exists(encounter_id) AND attribute_not_exists(seq)` (encounter_ledger.py:165-171) and botocore retries DynamoDB calls automatically. Sequence: PutItem for seq=41 is committed by DynamoDB; the HTTP response is lost to a socket timeout; botocore retries the byte-identical request; DynamoDB answers ConditionalCheckFailedException; `_persist` raises SequenceTaken; the retry loop at :322-328 re-reads the tail, finds seq=41 (its own entry), and writes an entry with identical inputs/output/tick_id at seq=42. Two identical predictions, same tick, chain verifies clean, and no downstream check can distinguish them from two genuine scores. This survives the design's tail-only rewrite untouched, because the duplicate is generated INSIDE record(), below the tick_id gate. It needs a content-idempotency check (compare the candidate's digest payload minus seq/prev_hash against the tail before writing) and the design has none.

THE 'MISSED CADENCE IS A LEDGER EVENT' CLAIM HAS A HOLE THAT IS INVISIBLE AND UNRECOVERABLE. The retrospective gap detector only writes a cadence_gap on chains that already have a roster item AND are re-scored later, and the heartbeat records missing TICKS, not missing PATIENTS. A 6-hour outage (rule disabled by a console mis-click, IAM change, reserved-concurrency throttle storm, region event) at 119 visits/day means roughly 30 patients arrive and are discharged entirely within the gap. They were never enrolled, so there is no roster item, no chain, no cadence_gap, no encounter_closed — zero trace. The only reconstruction path is the patients table, and backend/db/storage.py:29 TTLs it at 24h while backend/routers/patients.py:190 drops it to 30 MINUTES once a clinician marks the patient seen, with the sweep landing up to ~48h late (patients.py:197-199). So the evidence needed to even count what was missed is destroyed before anyone reads the heartbeat chain. Week 14 can say 'we missed 72 ticks' and cannot say 'we missed 30 patients', and the under-triage denominator shrinks silently in the flattering direction. Worse, the terminal case: if the programme dies on day 60 and never restarts, no later observer exists to record anything, and the sole detector is a CloudWatch alarm (Invocations < 250/24h) publishing to an SNS topic whose email subscription the codebase cannot confirm was ever accepted — a control living only in the AWS console, which is the exact anti-pattern this design correctly indicts solace-warmer for. The honest fix is an out-of-band arrival counter written at enrolment time and a dead-man's-switch that is itself in the ledger, not a graph.

THE DEPLOYED SHADOW CODE DRIFTS FROM THE TESTED CODE FOR 90 DAYS. `solace-shadow` is created once from 'the current solace-api image digest', and buildspec.yml's post_build runs `aws lambda update-function-code --function-name solace-api` and nothing else. Nothing in files_to_change touches buildspec.yml. Every subsequent CI deploy updates solace-api and leaves solace-shadow pinned to whatever digest existed at setup time — including, plausibly, an image predating the tail-only sequencing fix, the fabrication-bug fix at encounter_ledger.py:327, and the pagination fix. CI runs the full suite green against code the shadow function is not running. For a programme whose entire product is evidentiary, the ledger will record `model_version` for the ML artifacts and nothing at all about which scorer build produced the entry.

HARDENING `_check_uncertainty` INTO `_check_prediction` CAN 500 A LIVE CLINICIAN ENDPOINT AFTER A PARTIAL WRITE. `MissingUncertainty` subclasses ValueError (encounter_ledger.py:63) and routers/triage.py:114 catches ONLY `LedgerUnavailable`. The design adds four new rejection conditions (coverage a float in (0,1], non-empty conformal_set, non-empty coverage_source, non-empty output['top_features']) to the shared write path and asserts 'Verified the existing caller already satisfies all four, so this is not a breaking change' — but it verified the call-site SHAPE, not the runtime values. `top_features` comes from `_shap_top_features` (triage_ml.py:651+), which reshapes raw LightGBM pred_contrib output; any artifact whose feature_names disagree with the booster, or a future k<=0, yields []. When it does, refine_triage raises out of the try, AFTER `storage.update_patient` at line 78 has already written refined_esi_level to the patient row and BEFORE `_wf.fire` at line 121 — a 500 to the clinician, a refined score on the ED board, and no workflow. Any tightening of this shared gate needs the caller's except clause widened in the same change, and the design does not list routers/triage.py as modified.

THE CENSUS IS A SELF-SELECTED SUBSET, SO THE WEEK-14 NUMBER DOES NOT MEASURE THE DEPARTMENT. Enrolment reads solace-patients, and `storage.put_patient` has exactly ONE caller in the entire application: routers/intake.py:302. Every row in that table is a patient who completed Solace's own self-serve intake form. 'Re-score EVERY patient currently in the department' is therefore unachievable by construction — walk-ins who never touched the kiosk, EMS arrivals, and anyone triaged straight to a bed are invisible, and they are disproportionately the high-acuity patients an under-triage study is about. The design's weakest_point section names the vitals-staleness problem honestly but never states that the denominator itself is wrong; it treats the census as complete and spends its uncertainty budget on closure heuristics instead. This is the difference between 'the cadence may be uninformative' and 'the study measures a different population than it claims'.

TWO GOVERNANCE OBLIGATIONS ARE SKIPPED SILENTLY RATHER THAN DECIDED. (a) Consent: services/shadow_scorer.py's stated import list is triage_ml, triage_floor, encounter_ledger, db.shadow_roster, db.storage, lib.audit, lib.tenancy — `lib.consent` is absent, and no file, test or doc records the decision. Staying outside SEC-004's derived closure means the RULE does not fire; it does not mean 90 days of automated scoring on identified patients needs no legal basis. `lib/consent.py:89-98` exists specifically for background paths with no patient present. The right output is an explicit written 'treatment and operations, no gate' with counsel's name on it, mirroring how CONSTITUTION.md:108-111 handles the structurally identical voice question — not silence. (b) IAM: scripts/iam_shadow_exec_policy.json as specified grants DynamoDB, S3-less audit and KMS, and NO `logs:CreateLogGroup` / `CreateLogStream` / `PutLogEvents`. If that is the only policy attached to solace-shadow-exec, the function emits no CloudWatch logs at all, which silently guts the observability half of the 42abe22 story and makes the per-encounter score_failed diagnostics unreadable. The policy also grants no s3:PutObject for lib/audit.py's CMK-encrypted archive half of COMP-002.
verdicts.verdict: Strong on the money question, weak on the evidence question — and the evidence is the entire product. The 42abe22 defence is the best part and it is genuinely good: a separate function, ReservedConcurrentExecutions=1, retries pinned to 0 in code in two places, a handler that structurally never raises, the daemon-thread-join budget rather than a between-steps deadline, a rule born DISABLED, the programme window enforced in Python rather than in a console, a real budget alarm, and the correct catch that the ten existing DynamoDB alarms are dimensioned on a metric (UserErrors) that has no TableName dimension. The worst-case ceiling arithmetic (288 x 120s x 2GB ~ $27.60/mo) is honest and the pre-flight items (describe-table on the ledger, simulate-principal-policy for PutItem, measure one warm predict) are exactly right. Enumeration is mechanically valid against the real schema: the GSI exists with created_at as RANGE, both Queries use explicit KeyConditionExpressions, both paginate, no scan, boto3 confined to db/. PERF-004, ARCH-002, ARCH-001, SEC-004 and PERF-002 all hold. But the design makes one architectural choice — writing shadow entries onto the clinical encounter's own hash chain, because encounter_id == patient_id — and that choice cascades into four separate failures it does not see: shadow entries reachable by any authenticated clinician, a filter that cannot suppress the model="event" entries (one of which prints which vitals are missing, a live clinical nudge), a filtered timeline whose seq numbers and prev_hash links no longer verify for exactly the studied cohort, and a tail-based idempotency key that a single nurse's refine-triage call turns into duplicate scores plus cadence_gap entries claiming tens of thousands of missed ticks. A separate `shadow#<patient_id>` namespace kills all four at once and costs nothing. Independently, the enrolment cursor is unsound: strict `>` against a one-second-granularity created_at over an eventually-consistent GSI with no lookback window permanently drops patients, and the design states the opposite as a guarantee. And the missed-cadence claim, examined hard, detects missing ticks but not missing patients — the arrivals lost to an outage leave no trace anywhere, because the only record of them is TTL-deleted within 24 hours (30 minutes once seen). Not buildable as written. Buildable after: a separate ledger namespace, a lookback cursor, model-filtered idempotency, a content-idempotency guard inside record(), buildspec wiring for the shadow function, a widened except in routers/triage.py, logs: permissions, and a written consent determination. The core skeleton — one dedicated function, one tick, one roster, IAM as the shadow boundary — is the right skeleton and worth keeping.

verdicts.design_name: SHADOW-CADENCE — sharded roster with a conductor/worker split
fatal_flaws: FATAL — THE ROSTER SCHEMA CANNOT HOLD MORE THAN ONE ENCOUNTER PER SHARD, AND THE DESIGN'S OWN ERROR HANDLING HIDES IT. The roster is PK `shard` (S) = `{hospital_id}#{crc32(encounter_id)%SHARDS:02d}`, SK `item_kind` (S) where the hot row is the LITERAL string "cadence". The claim CAS confirms it: `Key={"shard": shard, "item_kind": "cadence"}`. That is ONE cadence item per shard, not one per encounter. With SHARDS=4 and census 25, ~6 encounters hash into each shard and all six address the same DynamoDB item. Concretely: patients P1..P6 land in shard A#02. P1 enrols and writes the cadence row with encounter_id=P1. P2's enrol overwrites it (or is rejected). At tick time the due-index returns exactly one key for the shard; the worker GetItems it, sees encounter_id=P1, and claims with `ConditionExpression="next_due_at = :expected AND encounter_id = :eid"`. For P2..P6 that condition can never be satisfied — and the design explicitly says `ConditionalCheckFailedException` "means another worker already holds this tick. That is a normal outcome, not an error: the loser logs a counter and moves on." So 5 of 6 patients in every shard are never scored, forever, and the worker returns success on every invocation. Every downstream number in the design is built on the assumption this is one row per encounter: `BATCH_LIMIT=40`, the `while "LastEvaluatedKey" in resp` pagination loop, the 250-encounters-in-one-shard pagination test, the 9,000 scores/day cost model, and the sparse-index-cost argument. A shard containing at most two items paginates nothing. The SK must be `cadence#<encounter_id>`, and until it is, the enumeration strategy — the core of the design — does not work.

FATAL — THE COMPLETENESS GATE AND THE ABSENT VITALS FEED CANCEL EACH OTHER, SO THE PROGRAMME'S STEADY STATE IS TOTAL REFUSAL. The design adds a refusal gate: below `completeness_threshold` (0.4 of "the 16 vitals keys") and fresher than `MAX_VITALS_AGE` (4h), emit `refused_low_completeness` instead of a score. Verified against source: `VitalsBody` (backend/routers/triage.py:30-46) accepts only 12 fields — `mean_arterial_pressure`, `pulse_pressure`, `shock_index` and `bmi` are DERIVED inside `build_row`, never submitted — so measured completeness caps at 12/16 = 0.75 and the 0.4 threshold requires 7 of the 12 submittable fields (exactly a standard SBP/DBP/HR/RR/temp/SpO2/GCS set: sitting precisely ON the threshold, so a missing GCS refuses). More damning: intake writes NO vitals at all (backend/routers/intake.py:258-298 has no vitals key; services/triage.py:2-6 says so in its docstring), and the ONLY writer of `measured_vitals` is the clinician-triggered refine-triage form (routers/triage.py:76). So the actual lifecycle of an enrolled encounter is: enrol → completeness 0.0 → refusal every 4 minutes → a nurse maybe submits vitals once at hour 1 → ~45 ticks of bit-identical scores → vitals cross MAX_VITALS_AGE at hour 5 → refusals for the rest of the stay, including all boarding time up to the 36h max-LOS backstop. The ledger fills with ~9,000 refusal events per day and a small number of duplicate identical scores. The weakest_point section admits the scores would be identical; it never notices that its own gate means there are almost no scores to be identical. The week-14 under-triage rate and recognition delay would be computed over a handful of scores that all coincide with the moments a clinician already looked at the patient — which is the one thing that cannot measure recognition delay. Two mechanisms the design added independently destroy its own deliverable.

FATAL — THE MISS DETECTOR IS STRUCTURALLY BLIND TO EXACTLY THE FAILURE IT EXISTS TO RECORD. The design claims "a missed cadence is itself a ledger event, not a silent gap," implemented as: on the next visit, "the claim path detects `now > previous_due + 90s` and writes a `cadence_missed` event BEFORE the score." But the claim CAS runs BEFORE the predict and BEFORE the ledger write, and it SETs `next_due_at = :next`. Interleaving: at T0 worker A claims P1 (roster now says next_due_at = T0+240s, tick_count incremented, last_tick_id set). A then calls `encounter_ledger.record()`, which raises `LedgerUnavailable` (throttle, IAM deny on PutItem, or — per the repo's own unknown — the table never having been created by setup_aws.py). No score is written. The fallback `cadence_missed` event is ALSO an `encounter_ledger.record()` call to the SAME table, so it fails identically. At T0+240s worker B visits, computes `now > previous_due + 90s` where previous_due = T0+240s → FALSE. No miss recorded. Every ledger-write failure produces a gap that the design's own detector cannot see, because the claim already advanced the clock as if the tick succeeded. This inverts the ledger's stated purpose (encounter_ledger.py:102-109: "the gap reads as 'nothing happened to this patient' rather than 'we failed to write it down'"). The same hole covers whole-system outages: if the conductor is throttled, the ESM is disabled, the queue drains to the DLQ, or the region is down, nothing runs and therefore nothing records that nothing ran. The design's answer is CloudWatch alarms — that is monitoring, not evidence, and it is not in the tamper-evident chain the programme is selling. A correct design needs `last_successful_tick_id` written AFTER the ledger append, gap reconciliation derived from `enrolled_at`/`departed_at` at week 14 (absence as evidence), and an out-of-band durability signal that does not share a failure domain with the ledger.

FATAL — THE ABANDONED-THREAD BUDGET PATTERN LEAKS THE LEDGER'S GLOBAL LOCK AND PERMANENTLY WEDGES A WARM CONTAINER, SILENTLY. The design copies `backend/main.py:253-258` ("daemon thread joined with a timeout") and cites its rationale verbatim: "The thread is not killed — Python cannot — but Lambda freezes the container the moment the handler returns." That reasoning is sound for the warmer, which is fire-and-forget. It is wrong here, because Lambda FREEZES threads on return and THAWS them on the next invocation of the same container — it does not kill them. Verified: `backend/services/encounter_ledger.py:91` is a module-global `threading.Lock`, and `:299` acquires it around `_chain()` (a ConsistentRead Query) and `_persist()` (a conditional PutItem) for all 8 retry attempts. The design never proposes removing it. Interleaving: worker invocation 1 runs the tick body on a daemon thread; that thread enters `record()`, acquires `_lock`, and blocks inside `_persist()` on a throttled DynamoDB PutItem for longer than `INVOCATION_BUDGET`; the main thread's `join(timeout=...)` returns, the handler returns success, the container freezes with `_lock` held. Invocation 2 arrives on the same warm container: its tick thread calls `record()`, blocks on `with _lock` forever (the holder is still parked on a socket read), the invocation budget expires, the handler returns SUCCESS, and a second thread is abandoned. Every subsequent message on that container scores zero patients and reports success. Reserved concurrency 6 means up to six containers can enter this state and never recover until Lambda recycles them (up to hours). Secondary version of the same bug: a thread abandoned mid-predict thaws during a LATER invocation, completes, and appends a ledger entry whose `observed_at` is from a tick 4-8 minutes earlier, landing AFTER a newer entry — producing a chain with non-monotonic `observed_at` and `recorded_at >> observed_at`, which reads to an auditor as backdating. Layer-2 tick_id dedupe does not catch it (the tail is a different tick_id), so it is admitted.

A BARE NUMBER CAN STILL REACH THE LEDGER, VIA THE EVENT EXEMPTION THE DESIGN ITSELF KEEPS OPEN. The design's structural claim is `record_score()` + a frozen `ScoreEntry` so the scorer "cannot construct a bare number to pass." But the AST callee allowlist in test_plan item 2 explicitly permits BOTH `encounter_ledger.record_score` AND `encounter_ledger.record`, and `_check_uncertainty` (encounter_ledger.py:253-255) exempts `model == "event"` by exact string match with no inspection of `output`. The scorer must retain `record()` for its five event kinds (`cadence_missed`, `refused_low_completeness`, `tenant_mismatch`, `scoring_quarantined`, `departed_max_los`). Nothing in the design or its tests prevents `record(model="event", model_version="shadow", output={"kind": "...", "esi_level": 3})` — a bare ESI, no conformal set, no coverage, no attribution, permanently in the tamper-evident record and indistinguishable from a real score to the week-14 analysis. The design's own prose says "MUST NOT pass model='event' for a score," but the enforcement is a sentence, not a test. There is no assertion that event outputs contain no scoring keys, and no assertion that the shadow package's `record()` calls are confined to `model="event"`. Requirement 2 is not met.

SEPARATELY: HARDENING `_check_uncertainty` AND ADDING `_check_attribution` INTRODUCES A NEW UNCAUGHT EXCEPTION CLASS ON A LIVE CLINICIAN ENDPOINT. `_check_attribution` is specified to require non-empty `output["top_features"]` for "any model starting with `triage_ml`" — which matches the EXISTING caller at backend/routers/triage.py:90 (`model="triage_ml"`), not just the new `triage_ml.shadow`. That caller wraps `record()` in `except encounter_ledger.LedgerUnavailable:` ONLY (routers/triage.py:114). `MissingUncertainty` subclasses `ValueError`, not `LedgerUnavailable`. `_shap_top_features` (triage_ml.py:651-663) can return a short or empty list under a degraded artifact (lgbm_only mode, empty `feature_names`), and coverage-value validation adds a second new raise path. The result is an unhandled 500 on `POST /patients/{id}/refine-triage` — a clinician-facing triage endpoint — where today the failure is logged and the clinician still gets their score. The test plan tests the new gate; it does not test that the existing caller survives it.

THE SHADOW GUARANTEE LEAKS THROUGH `GET /encounters/{id}/verify` AND THROUGH THE `checked` FIELD OF `timeline`, AND THE PROPOSED FIX BREAKS THE CHAIN'S OWN VERIFIABILITY. Verified: backend/routers/encounters.py has TWO clinician-authenticated endpoints. The design's fix names only `timeline` ("the router gains an explicit exclusion of models in SHADOW_MODELS"), and its test (`test_the_clinician_timeline_never_shows_a_shadow_score`) only exercises `timeline`. But (a) `GET /encounters/{patient_id}/verify` returns `{"ok", "checked", "broken_at", "reason"}` with no model filter at all — `checked=76` versus `checked=1` tells any authenticated clinician exactly which patients are under shadow scoring and how many times, which is a disclosure the programme promised not to make; and (b) `timeline` ALSO returns `verified`/`checked`/`broken_at` computed by `encounter_ledger.verify(patient_id)` over the UNFILTERED chain, so filtering `entries` yields a response asserting `checked: 76` alongside one visible entry. Worse, `_serialize`'s own docstring states the hashes are included "so somebody who does not trust us can recompute the chain themselves from the same fields, which is the difference between a log and a record" — removing shadow entries leaves surviving entries whose `prev_hash` points at hashes absent from the response, so any external party recomputing the filtered chain gets a broken link. The leak fix destroys the tamper-evidence property on the only endpoint that exposes it.

THE SHADOW-001 GUARANTEE TEST DOES NOT COVER THE FILE THAT OWNS THE INVOCATION. The import closure is seeded at `services.shadow` and the AST callee allowlist walks `backend/services/shadow/`. But `backend/shadow_handler.py` — listed first in files_to_change, owning both Lambda entrypoints, the budget, the PROGRAMME_END kill, and the calls into `db.shadow_dispatch` — sits at `backend/`, outside both. Nothing stops a future edit adding `storage.update_patient(...)`, `workflows.engine.fire(...)`, `httpx.post(...)` or an `include_router` to that file with every SHADOW-001 assertion still green. The design's own framing ("the product promise is 'no code path exists'") requires the closure seed to be the entrypoint module, not a package it imports. Same gap for `db/shadow_roster.py`, `db/ledger_store.py` and `db/shadow_dispatch.py`, none of which are in the allowlist's scope.

IT CANNOT REPEAT 42abe22'S BILL, BUT IT CONVERTS THAT INCIDENT'S LOUD FAILURE INTO A SILENT ONE, AND ADDS NO ALARM ON THE PRODUCT'S ONLY OUTPUT. The cost controls are genuinely good — retries pinned to 0 in committed code with an AST test, `ReservedConcurrentExecutions` (1/6) as a physical ceiling with a stated $415/mo worst case, SQS instead of async invoke, an EndDate, a handler hard-kill, and a Budgets alarm. Credit where due. But the design's stated safety property — "the worker NEVER returns a failure for a per-patient problem... a per-patient error rate of 100% still produces a 0% invocation error rate" — means every failure mode in this list (schema collision, universal completeness refusal, lock-wedged containers, LedgerUnavailable on every write, an unbuilt ledger table) presents as: nominal invocation count, zero errors, zero throttles, empty DLQ, queue draining normally, Duration well under timeout, spend on budget. Every alarm the design adds (Errors ≥ 1, Duration p99, Invocations > 1.5x envelope, DLQ depth, queue age) is blind to all of it. What caught 42abe22 was that the failure was loud in the metrics (1,080 errors on 1,080 invocations, a visible 3x); this design deliberately removes that loudness and puts nothing in its place. There is NO alarm on ledger writes per interval, no alarm on the ratio of scores to refusals, no per-shard freshness check, and no independent reconciler. For a 90-day programme whose sole deliverable is ledger rows, an emitted-rows-per-5-minutes alarm (and a daily reconciliation of roster-expected versus ledger-actual) is the one alarm that matters and it is absent.

THE CADENCE ARITHMETIC CONTRADICTS ITSELF BY 4x BETWEEN THE COST MODEL AND THE TEST PLAN, AND THE UNDERLYING LATENCY IS AN UNBENCHMARKED GUESS. The trigger section says the conductor runs `rate(1 minute)` and enqueues one message per (hospital, shard) "on a deterministic stagger so each shard is visited every 4 minutes" — 4 shards x 15 visits/hr x 24h = 1,440 worker invocations/day, matching the 43,200/month cost line. But the test plan asserts `test_a_50_hospital_shape_test`: "seed 50 programme rows x 4 shards, run one conduct tick, assert EXACTLY 200 SQS sends." 200 sends per one-minute tick means every shard is visited every minute, not every four — 4x the worker invocations (8.64M SQS messages/month, blowing the 1M free tier that the design counts on for its $0 SQS line, and ~$680/mo Lambda at 50 hospitals rather than the stated $270). One of the two is wrong and the design does not say which. Compounding it, the whole per-tick budget rests on "~300ms warm" per predict, which the design's own load-rehearsal gate concedes is unmeasured: `predict()` runs 2 TF-IDF transforms plus 5 LightGBM + 5 XGBoost + 5 CatBoost + 5 MLP forward passes plus a meta-learner plus a separate LightGBM `pred_contrib` SHAP pass, on arm64. At 1.5s — entirely plausible — `BATCH_LIMIT=40` needs 60s of pure CPU and the 90s invocation budget truncates every batch, producing a permanent backlog that the miss detector (see above) systematically under-records.

THE CONSENT DECISION THE MAP DEMANDED BE MADE EXPLICITLY IS SILENTLY DECIDED AND NEVER WRITTEN DOWN. This is HIPAA-regulated clinical software processing PHI continuously for 90 days. The design argues correctly that SEC-004's derived scope does not reach `triage_ml` (verified: services/triage.py imports only services.triage_engine, and triage_ml imports no provider leaf), and that no route exists. It then concludes nothing further is needed — but never states that conclusion, never cites a legal basis (treatment-and-operations vs QI vs IRB research), and omits `consent.for_patient` (backend/lib/consent.py:89-98, which exists precisely for "paths where the patient is not present to answer") from the scorer's AST callee allowlist, thereby making a consent check a test FAILURE if anyone later adds one. The constitution's own precedent for a structurally identical question is to ship a setting and defer to the deploying hospital's counsel (CONSTITUTION.md:108-111, VOICE_CONSENT_MODE), not to decide by omission. Compounding it: `routers/intake.py` is modified to call `services.shadow.roster.enrol(...)` on the synchronous, revenue-critical intake path with no stated try/except and no stated best-effort semantics, so a DynamoDB throttle on the roster becomes a 500 on patient intake.

MASSIVE COMPLEXITY FOR EVIDENCE THE DESIGN ITSELF ARGUES IT CANNOT PRODUCE. Two Lambda functions, an SQS queue plus DLQ plus event-source mapping, EventBridge Scheduler, two new DynamoDB tables, a sparse GSI, CRC32 sharding, leases, a compare-and-swap protocol, four independent idempotency layers, exponential-backoff quarantine, a changed hash digest on the tamper-evidence primitive, a persistence-layer relocation, 4 new backend modules, 6 modified files including three routers, 3 modified scripts, and 6 new test files — all to deliver, per the design's OWN weakest_point, "the same number written down 675,000 times" against a population that is a self-selected subset of the department (routers/intake.py:302 is the only caller of `storage.put_patient`; there is no ADT ingest). The design names this trade honestly and picks provable cadence over efficiency, which is worth real credit. But it then proceeds to ship the machinery anyway, when its own analysis identifies the ADT + Observation feed as the gating deliverable. The correct sequencing is: build and validate the feed, THEN decide the cadence shape. Shipping this first buys 90 days of a cryptographically chained record of refusal events.

SMALLER, STILL REAL: (a) The design refactors `encounter_ledger.py` — tail-based sequencing, relocated persistence, changed digest, hardened gates, new `verify()` semantics — against a module whose durable path has ZERO test coverage today (all 37 tests pass in 0.13s with no credentials at `solace_mode="local"`), with no golden production record to check against and no confirmation the ledger table even exists. Its own test plan admits `aws dynamodb describe-table` has never been run. (b) `verify()`'s new "expected-length check" has no specified source of truth; the only cheap one is the tail's `seq`, which the design never names. (c) The due-index is KEYS_ONLY, so each visit costs N GetItems on the roster plus N `storage.get_patient` reads against solace-patients — roughly 18,000 reads/day omitted entirely from the $0.40 roster line and the cost model. (d) `audit.record` per score adds 9,000 DynamoDB writes/day, also uncosted, and creates an admin-visible metadata trail of which patients are enrolled. (e) `VisibilityTimeout=720` against a 240s cadence means a redelivered message can carry a tick_id three ticks stale; the CAS prevents double-scoring but the design never says what a stale-tick worker writes. (f) `timeline()` on a clinician endpoint now performs a full paginated read plus `verify()` over chains of up to 540 entries for a 36h boarder, then discards most of them — a PHI-movement and latency regression on a route whose module docstring specifically split `verify` out to avoid exactly that.
verdicts.verdict: REJECT AS SPECIFIED — REWORK REQUIRED BEFORE BUILD. This is a serious, well-researched design and by far the strongest part of it is the 42abe22 remediation: retries pinned to zero in committed code with an AST test, reserved concurrency as a physical ceiling with a stated worst-case dollar figure, SQS instead of async invoke, a Scheduler EndDate plus a handler hard-kill, and a Budgets alarm the repo has never had. It correctly refuses the warmup-branch collision without amending PERF-002, correctly refuses to write refined_esi_level or fire the workflow engine, correctly moves ledger boto3 into db/, correctly stays off the four SEC-004 provider leaves (verified: services/triage.py imports only triage_engine), correctly adds no cross-tenant enumeration primitive, and correctly identifies its own weakest point in writing. It will not repeat the cost incident. But it fails on four independent counts that each stop the programme from producing its deliverable. (1) The roster data model physically cannot represent more than one encounter per shard — SK is the literal string \"cadence\" — and the design's own rule that a failed CAS is \"a normal outcome, not an error\" turns that into five of six patients silently never scored while the worker reports success. (2) The completeness gate the design adds, combined with the vitals feed it admits does not exist, makes refusal the steady state: the ledger fills with refusal events and almost no scores, so recognition delay is measurable only at the moments a clinician already looked. (3) The miss detector cannot see the failure it exists for, because the claim advances next_due_at before the ledger write, so every LedgerUnavailable produces a gap the system is structurally blind to — and the miss event shares a failure domain with the thing that failed. (4) The abandoned-thread budget pattern is imported from a fire-and-forget warmer into a path that holds a module-global lock across a DynamoDB round trip; Lambda thaws frozen threads on the next invocation, so one parked writer wedges a warm container permanently, silently, at 100% reported success. Add to that: a bare number still reaches the ledger through the model=\"event\" exemption the allowlist keeps open; the shadow guarantee leaks through GET /encounters/{id}/verify and through timeline's own checked field, and the proposed filter breaks the chain's external verifiability; the SHADOW-001 test does not cover shadow_handler.py, the file that owns the invocation; and the cost model contradicts its own test plan by 4x on a latency figure nobody has measured. Do this instead, in order: (a) build and validate the ADT + Observation feed first — it is the gating deliverable and the design says so; (b) fix the roster SK to cadence#<encounter_id>; (c) move the claim's success marker to after the ledger append and add an independent reconciler that derives gaps from roster enrolment rather than trusting a counter written by the component that failed; (d) drop the abandoned-thread pattern for anything that can hold the ledger lock, or remove the lock as part of the tail-read refactor; (e) confine the shadow package to record_score and assert that its record() calls carry no scoring keys; (f) alarm on ledger rows written per interval, which is the only signal that would catch any of the above. Then re-review. Until the feed exists, the honest cheap design is the one this document already describes and rejects: score on input-change plus a slow heartbeat, no shards, no leases, no SQS.

verdicts.design_name: Tick–Claim–Commit: a dedicated shadow-scorer Lambda with a DynamoDB-arbitrated per-(encounter, tick) lease
fatal_flaws: RECONCILE IS UNARBITRATED AND MANUFACTURES FALSE GAP EVENTS. The loop is reconcile -> claim -> score -> commit, so the CAS sits in the MIDDLE. The reconcile predicate (`last_claimed_tick > last_committed_tick` => write `claimed_not_committed`) cannot distinguish 'a tick died' from 'a tick is in flight', and the design deliberately permits overlap (ReservedConcurrency=3, 'a slow tick must not block the next one, and the CAS makes overlap harmless'). Interleaving: t=0 container A reconciles clean, claims T-1 (roster: claimed=T-1, committed=T-2), enters a cold `triage_ml.predict` that takes 40s unpickling artifacts.pkl. t=300s container B receives tick T, reconciles encounter E, reads claimed=T-1 > committed=T-2, and appends a hash-chained `{"event":"shadow_gap","reason":"claimed_not_committed","tick_id":T-1}`. t=302s A completes and writes a valid score for T-1 and commits. The ledger now contains, for the same encounter and the same tick, both a score and a tamper-evident assertion that the tick was claimed and never committed. At week 14 that fabricated hole is indistinguishable from a real one, and it inflates exactly the denominator the under-triage rate is computed from. The duplicate-delivery variant needs no slowness at all: EventBridge Scheduler is at-least-once, two deliveries of tick T land 50ms apart, A claims, B reconciles 20ms later and writes a false `claimed_not_committed` for T, THEN loses the CAS and 'skips, silently and correctly'. The CAS protects the score, which was never the duplicated write; the unprotected reconcile is. The design also states reconcile 'then advances the commit pointer', so B can set committed=T-1 while A is mid-score, after which the two pointers no longer mean what the predicate assumes. FIX (structural, not a tweak): claim FIRST and run reconcile under the claim, and make the predicate lease-based -- `claimed > committed AND now - last_claimed_at > LEASE_TTL`. `last_claimed_at` is already written by the claim and is simply never read.

THE SHADOW GUARANTEE LEAKS THROUGH `model="event"`, AND THE DESIGN'S OWN TEST WOULD PASS. The filter added to routers/encounters.py drops entries whose `model` starts with `shadow.`. Every gap, refusal, failure, enrolment and discharge entry this design specifies uses `model="event"` -- verbatim, because that exact string is the ONLY bypass of `_check_uncertainty` (encounter_ledger.py:254). None of them are filtered. I read routers/encounters.py: `_serialize` returns full `inputs` and `output` for every entry and `GET /encounters/{pid}/timeline` is clinician-authenticated and returns the lot. So a clinician opening any enrolled patient's timeline sees seq 1 = `{"event":"shadow_enrolled","hospital_id":...,"inputs_snapshot":{transcript, medical_info}}` and then, every five minutes, `{"event":"refused_insufficient_input","completeness":0.33,"missing":["spo2","respiratory_rate"]}`. That last one is worse than programme disclosure: it is a clinical prompt ('something wanted to re-score this patient and could not because nobody has taken their sats in four hours') delivered to a clinician by a system whose entire promise is that it displays nothing and alerts nobody. `test_the_clinician_timeline_hides_shadow_entries` tests the `shadow.` prefix and would pass green over this. Related: `tenancy.require_patient` gates both encounter endpoints on `storage.get_patient`, so once the patient row TTLs the programme's own evidence becomes unreadable through its only read path -- day 5 under the design's 96h extension, not day 1.

`_emit_event` IS AN UNGUARDED BARE-NUMBER PATH BY CONSTRUCTION -- this is the direct answer to 'can a bare number reach the ledger under ANY path in this design': yes. `ShadowScore.__post_init__` guards `_emit`. `_emit_event` writes `model="event"`, and `_check_uncertainty` returns at encounter_ledger.py:254 before any validation, tightened or not. The AST test asserts only that `encounter_ledger.record(` appears nowhere outside `_emit`/`_emit_event`; nothing constrains what `_emit_event` puts in `output`. `_emit_event({"event":"score_failed","esi_level":3,"last_known":2})` is a bare ESI in the append-only clinical record with no uncertainty, no conformal set and no attribution, passing every test the design specifies including the tightened gate and the parametrized `test_a_bare_number_cannot_reach_the_ledger`. Needs a closed enum of permitted `event` values plus an assertion that no event output carries an `esi_level`-shaped key -- neither is present.

'MISSED CADENCE IS A RECORDED EVENT' IS NOT ACHIEVABLE AS SPECIFIED: BOTH RECOVERY PATHS ARE THE THING THAT IS DOWN. Gap recording happens at the next successful tick's reconcile. Shortfall recording happens in `roster.discharge()` -- called by an ADT feed that does not exist -- or by the max-LOS auto-discharge, which is executed BY the tick. Concretely: the schedule is disabled, or every invocation cold-starts past the 60s budget, or the poison path (flaw 7) tears down containers faster than they warm, starting day 80. No tick runs again before `EndDate` = day 91. Every encounter enrolled after day 80 carries an enrolment event and nothing else, forever -- not one gap row. The ledger asserts 'nothing happened to these patients', which encounter_ledger.py:102-109 names as the precise failure the ledger exists to prevent. The narrower and more likely version is worse for the report: an outage from T to T+n is recorded only for encounters still active at T+n, so in a 4h-LOS ED a 6h outage erases the entire cohort that passed through it with zero trace. `expected_ticks vs committed_ticks` on the discharge event does not save this because there is no discharge event either. Closing this needs a heartbeat chain written by something OTHER than the scorer (a per-hospital 'programme was alive at T' record), so absence in a score chain can be distinguished from absence in the world. No such mechanism exists here, and the only detector offered -- an Invocations-below-expected alarm -- is out-of-band, which is the same class as the console-only 42abe22 mitigations this design is a reaction to.

THE ENUMERATION CONTRADICTS ITS OWN JUSTIFICATION, AND THE ROSTER HAS NO WRITER. (a) The design rejects the patients GSI partly because an ALL projection 'makes the patients GSI drag transcripts and SHAP blobs', then specifies `active-index` as INCLUDE with `NonKeyAttributes=[...,"snapshot",...]` where `snapshot` is defined as {transcript, medical_info, language}. That is the transcript, dragged on every page of every tick, 288x/day, and duplicated into a second PHI copy at rest that the COMP-003/minimization narrative never accounts for. Either the snapshot is in the projection (and the criticism applies verbatim to its own index) or it is not (and every tick needs an extra point read per encounter, absent from the cost model). (b) `last_claimed_tick`/`last_committed_tick` are also in the projection, so every claim AND every commit rewrites the GSI item -- ~11,500 uncosted GSI writes/day. (c) Nothing calls `roster.enrol`. `routers/intake.py:302` is the only `put_patient` in the application and the design does not modify it; no file in `files_to_change` writes the roster. The sparse index returns zero items and the tick is a correct, well-tested, alarmed no-op. The design files this under `weakest_point` as a data-availability problem; it is also a missing component in its own file list.

THE DASHBOARD PAGINATION + TTL EXTENSION IS AN UNCOSTED, UNCEILINGED COST MULTIPLIER ON THE CLINICIAN HOT PATH -- the 42abe22 shape, reintroduced in the section that promises it cannot recur. The design (i) adds a `LastEvaluatedKey` loop to `_ddb_query_patients_by_hospital` (storage.py:181-187) and (ii) raises `_default_ttl` to 96h for shadow hospitals and skips the 30-minute drop at patients.py:190. I verified the index is `ProjectionType: ALL` (setup_aws.py:90) over the row built at intake.py:258-298 -- transcript, clinician_prebrief, clinical_scribe_note, differential, workup_orders, disposition, comfort_protocol, shap_values, photo_analysis, ai_processing_log -- fetched in full to build the 18 scalar fields of `_summary()` (patients.py:27-49). Today that read is capped at one 1MB page. After the change, at 119 admits/day with 96h retention the partition holds ~475 fat rows; at ~30KB that is ~14MB, and `usePollingPatients` fetches every 10s per open dashboard. Five dashboards = 43,200 polls/day, each now reading the whole partition: ~3,500 RCU/poll, ~151M RCU/day, roughly $38/day -- north of $1,100/month, on `solace-api`, which has no reserved concurrency, no Duration alarm and no budget alarm. The stated $3.30/month covers the scorer and none of this. Pagination there is correct and necessary; it requires a `ProjectionExpression` (or a re-projected index) and a `Limit` FIRST, and the design specifies neither.

THE POISON HANDLER CANNOT DO WHAT IT SAYS, AND ITS OWN TEST WILL FAIL. The design adds `_lock.acquire(timeout=5)` raising `LedgerUnavailable`, and separately says a poisoned container 'writes a `model="event"` gap entry for the current tick and then raises'. That gap entry is `encounter_ledger.record(...)`, which takes the same module-global lock the abandoned thread still holds (encounter_ledger.py:91, :299) -- so it raises `LedgerUnavailable` after 5s and the container raises having written nothing. `test_a_poisoned_container_kills_itself` asserts 'a gap event was written' and will fail against the design's own lock change. Recovery then falls back entirely to the next tick's reconcile, which flaw 1 shows is unsound.

TIGHTENING `_check_uncertainty` RAISES AN EXCEPTION CLASS THE ONLY PRODUCTION CALLER CANNOT CATCH. `MissingUncertainty` subclasses `ValueError` (encounter_ledger.py:63); I confirmed routers/triage.py:114 catches `encounter_ledger.LedgerUnavailable` only, and the comment above it explains the swallow is deliberate because the score is already in front of the clinician. Today the gate cannot fire on that path. After prerequisite (c) -- numeric coverage in (0,1], non-empty `conformal_set`, non-empty `output["top_features"]` -- any artifact or SHAP edge case (`_shap_top_features` reads `boosters[0]` and reshapes a `pred_contrib` array) converts a swallowed record-keeping failure into an unhandled 500 on a clinician-facing endpoint mid-triage. The design modifies routers/triage.py in the same change and does not widen that except clause. One-line fix; the reviewable failure is tightening a shared invariant without tracing its blast radius.

THE 'BELT AND BRACES' RETRY DEFENCE MAY BE HALF DECORATIVE, AND `verify_shadow_infra.py` WOULD REPORT IT HEALTHY. `put_function_event_invoke_config` governs ASYNCHRONOUS invocations only. Whether EventBridge Scheduler's Lambda target invokes async or `RequestResponse` decides whether the function-level `MaximumRetryAttempts=0` is load-bearing or inert -- and if it is `RequestResponse`, the 90s timeout also interacts with Scheduler's own per-invocation behaviour differently than modelled. The design asserts the setting via an AST test on the deploy script and reads it back via `get_function_event_invoke_config`, both of which will happily confirm a config nothing consults. That is a control that looks present and is not: precisely the failure mode this entire design exists to prevent, reproduced in its own headline defence. It belongs in the pre-flight verification list and is not there.

NO TENANCY CHECK ON THE ROW ACTUALLY SCORED, PLUS TWO SOURCES OF TRUTH FOR ENROLMENT. Step 3 is `storage.get_patient` (point GetItem by encounter_id) plus the roster snapshot. `tenancy.belongs_to` appears in the callee allowlist but nowhere in the described flow. A roster row with a stale or wrong `active_hospital` -- transfer, enrolment bug, or drift between `settings.shadow_hospital_ids` and the schedule's `Input.hospital_ids`, two independent sources of truth this design creates -- produces a cross-tenant read whose score is written into a hash-chained record that carries the hospital only inside a seq-1 event. SEC-008's derived test currently has an EMPTY unscoped set because it scans clinician ROUTES; a background job is not a route, so nothing would see this. That is the exact staleness mode CONSTITUTION.md:24-27 warns about.

ARCH-002 (L1) IS ENTRENCHED AT THE CHEAPEST POSSIBLE MOMENT TO FIX IT. The design substantially rewrites `backend/services/encounter_ledger.py` -- tail-read sequence allocation, pagination, lock timeout, LRU cache, validation, docstring removal -- and leaves `import boto3` / `boto3.resource(...).Table(LEDGER_TABLE)` at :125-129 inside `backend/services/`, which ARCH-002 (L1, scope `backend/services/*.py`) forbids and which CONSTITUTION.md cites `backend/db/storage.py:1` as the pattern for. Every ledger write in the 90-day programme goes through that call. Doing this refactor without moving persistence into `db/` makes the L1 violation permanent on the single module the entire compliance claim rests on. Note also that `backend/services/*.py` does not glob into `backend/services/shadow/`, so the new package's compliance is luck rather than enforcement.
verdicts.verdict:
Do not build the tick loop as specified. Do build the prerequisite ledger repairs and the infrastructure skeleton, which are overdue regardless of whether this programme ever runs.

What is genuinely right: the separate function is the correct answer to the PERF-002 collision and needs no constitutional amendment. The 42abe22 controls (retries 0 in code, reserved concurrency as a physical ceiling, schedule EndDate, DLQ, drift verification, alarms whose thresholds could actually have caught 3.75 errors per 5 minutes) are a materially better answer than the incident got. The three ledger prerequisites -- tail-based sequence allocation, removing the `or chain + [entry]` fabrication at :327, paginating `_load_all` -- are repairs the repo needs whether or not the shadow programme happens; the fabrication bug is the single worst thing in this codebase for a tamper-evidence claim and this design is the first artifact to name it precisely. The test plan is the strongest part of the submission: derived-scope closure with an empty allowlist, floor and staleness tests, the raise-only floor property test, the sweep invariant, and an opt-in real-DynamoDB integration test for a write path with literally zero coverage today.

What kills it: four of the seven questions asked come back negative. The idempotency story breaks under an interleaving the design explicitly invites -- the CAS is in the middle of the sequence and the reconcile that runs before it fabricates gap rows in the tamper-evident record under normal overlap and under normal duplicate delivery. A bare number does reach the ledger, through `_emit_event`, because `model="event"` is the one string that bypasses the gate and nothing constrains what an event's output holds. The shadow guarantee leaks, because every event entry the design writes uses that same string and the proposed filter matches `shadow.` -- so refusal events become a five-minute clinical prompt on a clinician-authenticated screen, under a test that passes. And 'a missed cadence is a recorded event' is unachievable as built: both recovery paths run inside the tick, so a sustained outage records nothing, and a short outage erases every encounter that arrived and departed inside it.

The cost analysis is careful about the scorer and blind about everything else. Pagination on `_ddb_query_patients_by_hospital` combined with a 4x TTL extension turns a 1MB-capped read into a full-partition read of ALL-projected rows carrying transcripts and scribe notes, on a path polled every 10 seconds per dashboard, with no ProjectionExpression, no Limit, no ceiling and no alarm -- plausibly two orders of magnitude above the scorer's entire bill, in the same document that argues the incident is arithmetically impossible.

The author's own weakest_point is honest and correct as far as it goes -- no vitals feed, no departure signal, no census ingestion -- but understates the conclusion. This is not a scheduler that will produce thin results; it is a scheduler with no writer for the table it enumerates. The enrolment path is absent from its own file list.

Sequence I would accept: (1) land the three ledger repairs plus the ARCH-002 move into db/ and the read-path error wrapping, with the integration test, as a standalone change -- highest value, lowest risk, independently justified; (2) land the infra skeleton (separate function, retries, concurrency, DLQ, EndDate, alarms, verify_shadow_infra) with a handler that writes one heartbeat entry and nothing else, to prove the seam; (3) resolve enrolment, the ADT/departure signal, and the vitals feed before writing a single scoring line; (4) redesign the tick as claim-first with a lease-TTL reconcile predicate, a closed event enum, and a timeline filter keyed on programme membership rather than a model-name prefix. Re-review at (4). The pre-flight list in the test plan should run before any of this: if `solace-encounter-ledger` was never created or the IAM allow was never attached, every production ledger write has been failing silently for months and the entire foundation is theoretical.

winner.design_name: Shadow Tick — one dedicated Lambda, one disabled-by-default EventBridge rule, one roster table
fatal_flaws: ENROLMENT SILENTLY DROPS PATIENTS — the cursor is unsound against the real schema. backend/db/storage.py:25 is `_now_iso()` with `timespec="seconds"`, so `created_at` has ONE-SECOND resolution, and the design queries `created_at > :since` with a strict `>` and advances the cursor to max(created_at) seen. Interleaving A (same-second collision): patients P1 and P2 both get created_at="2026-08-11T14:23:07Z"; the tick's Query at 14:23:07.4 returns only P1 (P2's put_patient lands at 14:23:07.8); cursor advances to ...07Z; the next tick queries `> ...07Z` and P2, sitting at exactly ...07Z, is excluded FOREVER. Interleaving B, worse and not rare: GSI reads are ALWAYS eventually consistent and DynamoDB gives no ordering guarantee on index propagation. P1 (created_at ...07Z) propagates to hospital_id-created_at-index at 14:23:10.5; P2 (created_at ...09Z) propagates at 14:23:09.1. The tick queries at 14:23:10.0, sees only P2, advances the cursor to ...09Z, and P1 is permanently invisible to every future tick. The design asserts verbatim that the cursor is 'advanced to max(created_at) actually seen, never to now, so nothing is skipped' — that claim is false. The dropped patient gets no roster item, no ledger entry, no cadence_gap and no encounter_closed; they are indistinguishable from a patient who never existed, which is precisely the population the under-triage rate is about. Fix is cheap and absent: subtract a lookback (cursor minus 2 ticks) and lean on the `attribute_not_exists(sk)` conditional put that is already there.

SHADOW SCORES ARE WRITTEN INTO THE CLINICAL ENCOUNTER'S OWN HASH CHAIN, and every downstream problem below flows from that one choice. encounter_id == patient_id everywhere (routers/triage.py:91, routers/clinical_ai.py:483, routers/encounters.py:74), and the design's own driven test asserts `encounter_ledger.timeline(pid)` gained one entry — same chain. Consequences, all concrete: (a) GET /api/{h}/encounters/{pid}/timeline (routers/encounters.py:56) returns every entry to any authenticated clinician at that hospital; the design's mitigation is to filter `model.startswith("shadow_")` out of the response. (b) `_serialize` (routers/encounters.py:35-52) emits `seq`, `prev_hash` and `entry_hash` per entry, and the endpoint's own docstring says these exist so 'somebody who does not trust us can recompute the chain themselves'. Filtering leaves seq 1,26,51... with prev_hash values that do not link, so an external verifier recomputing the displayed chain gets 'sequence gap'/'broken link' for every enrolled patient. The programme destroys the tamper-evidence property of the clinical record for exactly the cohort it studies. (c) GET .../verify (routers/encounters.py:83) returns `checked` = raw chain length; an enrolled patient shows ~25+/day against ~1 for everyone else, so enrolment and cadence are inferable with no entry content at all. Filtering entries does not fix a count. Using a separate encounter_id namespace (`shadow#<patient_id>`) would have made this whole class disappear — require_patient() would 404 the chain, verify() would stay honest, and the idempotency bug below would not exist.

THE `model="event"` ENTRIES DEFEAT THE LEAK FILTER AND ONE OF THEM IS A CLINICAL NUDGE. The uncertainty exemption at encounter_ledger.py:253-255 is an exact string match on `"event"`, so cadence_gap, score_refused_incomplete, rescore_no_input_change, encounter_closed and score_failed MUST be spelled `model="event"` — and therefore none of them match `model.startswith("shadow_")`. All five pass straight through the design's own filter into the clinician timeline. `{"kind": "score_refused_incomplete", "present": [...], "missing": ["spo2", "respiratory_rate"]}` rendered on a clinician's screen is a prompt to go take vitals on that patient. That is the shadow programme influencing care, which is the one thing the 90 days must not do. The design never notices that its exemption requirement and its filter requirement are in direct contradiction.

THE IDEMPOTENCY KEY IS UNREADABLE THE MOMENT ANY NON-SHADOW WRITER TOUCHES THE CHAIN, and the design's own tail-only optimization is what makes it unreadable. Duplicate suppression is `tail = tail(E); if tail.output.get("tick_id", -1) >= tick_id: skip`, where tail() is Query(ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1). Two live writers append to that same chain with no tick_id in `output`: routers/triage.py:90-113 (clinician refine-triage) and routers/clinical_ai.py:482-500 (ai-override event).
